item.title: REVIEW: The first batch of Android XR smartglasses made me rethink my stance on specs without displays
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The first batch of Android XR smartglasses made me rethink my stance on specs without displays I still want models with built-in screens, but Google’s first run of intelligent eyewear has a lot to offer. The first device powered by Android XR came out last year when Samsung released the Galaxy XR headset. But this fall, Google is taking its augmented reality platform in a different direction with the launch of intelligent eyewear from partners such as Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. This gives Google its own version of lightweight smartglasses to rival competitors like the third-gen Ray-Ban Meta line, and after testing them out, it made me reconsider my feelings about smart specs without built-in displays. As this first generation of intelligent eyewear is a bit of a departure from previous Android XR devices, I think it's important to get some of the basics out of the way first. For this family of specs, Google is in charge of the OS while Samsung is handling much of the tech — including things like the cameras, mics, touch sensors and more. All of that then gets handed over to Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, who are in charge of the glasses design, lenses, general sales and customer support. Right off the bat, this seems like a great division of responsibilities because it allows each company to do what they're best at. Google handles the software, Samsung takes care of the hardware and the real glasses makers ensure you have good-looking frames with the right prescriptions (you can even opt for transition/photochromic lenses). And right out of the gate, it feels like there's already a lot of interesting styles and color combos to choose from, regardless if you're a bit more fashion-forward or if you, like me, prefer a more traditional frame. Another important thing to note is that while Gentle Monster's eyewear will be a touch more expensive than Warby Parker's models ($449 and $395, respectively), they will have the same general tech specs. Those include the same 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage, a 12MP camera (that also handles up to 3K video), stereo speakers, far-field mics and a built-in touch sensor. Battery life is also the same across the board with around nine hours of use on a single charge, while the case for the glasses stores enough juice for multiple full charges. Furthermore, you won't be required to have a paid Gemini plan to use any of the features of the glasses; it's all free. These glasses will even work with both Android devices and iPhones with feature parity across both OSes. That said, there won't be any options with a built-in display, which means Google won't have a true rival to the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, at least not yet. When it comes to features, it's no surprise that these glasses have a lot of overlap with the Ray-Ban Meta specs. There's a physical button near the right temple for capturing images: A short press takes a picture while a long press records videos. There's also a touch sensor built into the right arm for doing stuff like controlling volume, pausing audio or dismissing Gemini. And of course, the glasses are connected to your phone wirelessly (either Bluetooth or Wi-Fi depending on the situation) so you have access to streaming music, notifications, messages, supported apps and more. However, the real lynchpin of the entire platform is Google's AI, which can be easily summoned via voice controls or by performing a long press on the touch panel. Now I'll admit that I don't interact with Gemini all that often when I'm using a phone or a laptop. When I already have access to a screen, a keyboard and all sorts of dedicated apps, so I find I can often perform tasks faster manually than asking an AI assistant to do them. But when wearing smartglasses, it's a whole different story. If you want to respond to a text, get turn-by-turn directions or start some tunes, you can do all that hands-free with simple voice commands while keeping your phone in your pocket. Granted, that is sort of table stakes for smartglasses these days, but being able to walk around with your head up while dodging traffic or other pedestrians can't be understated. But it goes deeper, because thanks to Gemini's intelligence and persistent memory between conversations, the AI in your glasses has a much deeper understanding of how to help you. Instead of constantly having to say a wake word all the time, you can have more natural back and forth dialogue. This allows you to get updates on your events, make adjustments to questions and pick up on previous queries even when they happen throughout the course of your day (you can specify how long you want Gemini to remember conversations). Where things get really interesting is the combination of computer vision and AI, which allowed me to do things like pick up a physical invite card and simply ask Gemini to add it to my calendar. No need to grab my phone, open up an app and add details like the time, date and location myself. I was also able to do things like simply look at a bunch of different ingredients and ask Gemini to make a smoothie from what was in front of me. It can even do rough estimates for how much of a certain food has been added, so if you're not worried about being super precise, you can leave your measuring cups in a drawer. And if you run out of certain foods, you can easily tell Gemini to add something to your grocery list. Then there are other features like live translation, which feels kind of magical. The glasses are designed so that the mics are directed in a cone-shaped space in front of you, so that even in a room with other conversations going on, the glasses don't get confused. Not only does this let you switch speakers naturally just by looking at someone else, Gemini will even adjust the output of a translation to sound similar to the original speaker. This allows you to follow along in real-time almost as well as someone who speaks the language naturally. That said, the thing that impressed me the most about these Android XR glasses is the platform itself. Compared to some rivals where a lot of features feel like a work in progress, Google's OS feels much more mature. This includes little touches like dedicated sounds when Gemini accesses your camera, when the glasses take a photo or video, when Gemini leverages external AI and more. Google has done a pretty good job of translating a lot of the most important features you use on your phone to a medium without a screen. Then there's Google's approach to privacy, which looks to be a step up from the competition. In addition to each pair of glasses coming with an LED indicator that blocks you from taking pictures or videos when it's covered up or disabled, Google also isn't supporting features like livestreaming video directly from the specs. Furthermore, Google says images and info sent to Gemini will stay on your device and will not be used to train AI or for ad targeting. That might not sound like much, but considering Google owns YouTube and generates billions from advertising, the simple act of leaving money on the table in favor of privacy is a welcome departure from Meta's glasses. Those have always felt like they are meant to expand the reach of Facebook and Instagram. The one caveat to all this is that you do have to buy into talking to and relying rather heavily on Gemini. I'm still not sure I'm 100 percent on board with that, but at least for me, these glasses make a better argument for always-on AI support than almost any other class of device I've used. So while I'm still waiting for companies to deliver streamlined specs with built-in displays, these audio-first options feel like much more than a stepping stone towards that. They're surprisingly full-featured, and I don't think it's a stretch to say that compared to rival assistants like Siri, Muse and others, Gemini is the smartest of the bunch. So even if you primarily want these for playing music, keeping tabs on your schedule and getting occasional help from AI, Google's first batch of Android XR-powered intelligent eyewear feels like it's already jumped to the front of the pack. Pre-orders for the new family of Android XR intelligent eyewear from both Warby Parker and Gentle Monster begin today with official sales slated for December 10.

item.title: REVIEW: TCL Tab A1 Plus Review: An Affordable Tablet, But Not an Exceptional One
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The $279.99 TCL Tab A1 Plus has an enormous 12.2-inch screen. In fact, it's about the least you'll pay for a screen this large. It also has a sleek design, helpful AI tools, and solid audio. But it struggles to open certain apps thanks to slow performance, has a disappointing four-hour battery life, and uses outdated wireless radios. Rather than opt for the TCL Tab A1 Plus, we recommend the $259.99 Lenovo Idea Tab Plus for its brighter screen, longer battery life, and lower price for affordable tablets. The A1 Plus sports a sleek aluminum unibody design in Aerolite Grey, the tablet's sole colorway. I'd call it gunmetal-esque. Its most defining feature is a circular camera module on the back, a signature of TCL's design language. Flip it over in landscape mode, and you'll find the selfie camera centered within a thick black bezel that frames the display. On the top-left edge, you'll find the power button and volume rocker. On the top-right edge is a slot for microSD cards up to 2TB. On the left and right edges, you'll find a pair of speakers, with a USB-C port on the right. The A1 Plus caught my eye with its impressively slim profile. It measures 10.85 by 7.45 by 0.26 inches (HWD) and weighs 1.19 pounds. Meanwhile, the IdeaPad Tab Plus, which measures 10.98 by 7.13 by 0.25 inches and weighs 1.17 pounds, is taller, narrower, slightly thicker, and a hair heavier. The 11-inch iPad is more compact and lighter at 9.79 by 7.07 by 0.28 inches and 1.05 pounds. The A1 Plus easily slides into tight backpack sleeves, but the iPad is more portable. It's worth noting that the A1 Plus has an IP54 rating, which means it's protected against light dust buildup and water splashes. Neither the Lenovo nor the Apple tablets have IP certifications. The A1 Plus has a 12.2-inch, 2,400-by-1,600-pixel LCD with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. While testing the tablet on YouTube, I expected a 1440p viewing option, but it's capped at 1080p. This is because the processor can only handle video playback at 1080p60 at its max. Sharpness isn't the A1 Plus's strongest suit, but the screen still pumps out surprisingly vibrant, colorful visuals. Taking the A1 Plus for a spin outside, the 550-nit display struggles to be visible in sunlight—and the high-glare glass doesn't help. I was frustrated by the ceiling lights of my local library, which reflected off the glossy panel. If you're an outdoorsy tablet user, or someone who frequently works under harsh overhead lighting, you might want to consider another option. The 12.1-inch, 2,560-by-1,600-pixel IdeaPad Plus features a 90Hz display with a peak brightness of 800 nits. The iPad's 2,360-by-1,640-pixel display, on the other hand, maxes out at 60Hz and 500 nits of brightness. The A1 Plus doesn't ship with a stylus, but it's compatible with the $59.99 TCL T-Pen 2, which you can purchase separately. I didn't get a chance to test it. If you're seeking a more flexible display option, the $299.99 Tab A1 Plus Nxtpaper relies on the company's Nxtpaper screen tech, which delivers a glare-free experience and multiple viewing modes, including monotone for reading. Inside, you'll find the Snapdragon 4 Gen 2 chip, a four-nanometer, octa-core processor. The tablet is configured with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, though that can be expanded up to 2TB via microSD. TCL makes only this one version of the tablet. I noticed its sluggish performance right away, with some lag when firing up apps. Furthermore, it runs hot even during the simplest tasks, such as playing music on Spotify or downloading a mobile game. I was curious to test the TCL tablet to get its benchmark scores, which is how we compare devices. Geekbench 6 generated single- and multi-core scores of 895 and 2,197, respectively. This is pretty unremarkable, but it beats the MediaTek Dimensity 6400-equipped Idea Tab Plus, which posted scores of 756 and 1,969. The A16-packed iPad blew both out of the water, with 2,479 and 4,352. I also ran the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme test. The A1 Plus scored 181 overall at just 1.08 frames per second (fps). This is worse than the Idea Tab Plus (341 frames at 2.04fps) and the iPad (2,599 frames at 15.6fps). As expected from a device hovering around one frame per second in stress tests, a graphics-heavy title like Genshin Impact suffered massive visual compromises, triggering microstutters that routinely threw off my combat timing. Unsurprisingly, just 10 minutes of gameplay causes noticeable heat to develop, though it never becomes uncomfortably hot. TCL equipped the A1 Plus with an 8000mAh battery; it supports wired charging up to 20W. This is an average-sized battery for a tablet in this price range. While using the A1 Plus, it seemed to burn through power pretty quickly, and unfortunately, my tests confirmed those suspicions. I ran PCMag’s battery rundown test, which involves streaming a 1080p video over Wi-Fi with the screen at maximum brightness. The A1 Plus lasted a disappointing 4 hours and 28 minutes on a single charge—well behind the Idea Tab Plus (6 hours and 19 minutes) and iPad (6 hours and 43 minutes). To make matters worse, getting the A1 Plus to 100% is painfully slow, even with a compatible fast-charging charger. In 15 minutes, it only charged to 12%. In 30 minutes, it only reached 18%. A full charge took a little over three hours. The A1 Plus features Bluetooth 5.0 and Wi-Fi 5, and TCL doesn't offer a model with cellular support. Keep in mind that the Idea Tab Plus (Bluetooth 5.2, Wi-Fi 5) and the iPad (Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, sub-6GHz 5G, gigabit LTE, and GPS) have more up-to-date connectivity specs. When connected to and placed near a Wi-Fi 6 router in my office, the A1 reached maximum download and upload speeds of 156Mbps and 140Mbps, respectively. I launched the same speed test on the M4 iPad Air in the same location. It posted much better speeds of 229Mbps down and 163Mbps up. Moving to the fringes of my Wi-Fi network to really test the tablets' radios, the A1 Plus sputtered, with download and upload speeds of 21.2Mbps and 21.9Mbps, respectively. The iPad fared much better, reaching 154Mbps down and 70.9Mbps up. TCL promises up to 81dB from its quad speakers, but the tablet beat that estimate in my sound testing. Cranked to max volume while playing PCMag’s test track, The Knife's "Silent Shout," the A1 Plus peaked at 85.4dB. The audio quality is better than expected, too, delivering clear, punchy sound that doesn't turn into a buzzy, tinny mess at max volume. It's a rare treat for a sub-$300 tablet. TCL equipped the A1 Plus with two cameras: an 8MP rear shooter and a 5MP front-facing camera. My expectations for these cameras were already quite low. After all, budget tablets aren't known for their camera systems. As it turns out, I was right. The A1 Plus does a decent job with color accuracy. For example, check out the array of books below. From the mustard-yellow Mad Honey novel to the teal When I Ran Away book, the 8MP camera captured the books' hues quite well. However, the shot lacks fine texture due to soft focus and over-smoothing. Take a look at this photo of this celestial globe. Other than the months on the rings, I can't make out any other text in this picture. It's all too blurry and out of focus. On the plus side, however, the camera does a good job at reproducing the globe's striking blue color. The rosy-pink color, contrasting with the green of this flower, may make this photo look good at a glance, but the camera struggles with harsh sunlight, resulting in blown-out highlights and white splotches. The A1 Plus does a better job with selfies. It's not the sharpest nor the crispest, but there's no need to capture every single detail on one's face. There's some softness, but the selfie camera is decent for personal video calls and quick snapshots. The A1 Plus ships with Android 16 and is set to receive Android 17, along with three years of security updates. While the Idea Tab Plus matches the TCL tablet's security patching schedule, Lenovo promises an extra year of OS upgrades, keeping it current through Android 18. The iPad beats both tablets, offering an expected minimum of five years of software updates. There’s a whole suite of Google apps preloaded onto the A1 Plus, including the standards, such as Gmail, Maps, and YouTube. There's also support for Circle to Search, which lets you look up anything on your screen by pressing and holding the center circle button. You can invoke Gemini by pressing and holding the power button, making it easy to query the AI assistant, kick off voice conversations, or ask questions about whatever is on your screen. TCL has its own suite of AI-powered productivity tools. For example, there's Text Assist, which lets you highlight and drag anything you're reading to the bottom of the display to access three straightforward actions: Explain, Translate, and Rewrite. You can launch Writing Assist with a three-finger upward swipe gesture, which pulls up a handful of writing preset options, including email composing, event planning, outlining, and more. There’s also Smart Translator, which facilitates face-to-face conversations across 15 downloadable languages, including Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Turkish. Overall, TCL's software package isn't doing anything groundbreaking, but features like Text Assist are genuinely useful. Being able to translate, break down, or rewrite text right on your screen saves you the extra step of invoking Gemini or opening ChatGPT. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The TCL Tab A1 Plus is one of the cheapest big-screened Android tablets you can buy. While we like how large and vivid the screen is, along with the classy design and solid AI, it falls short elsewhere. The slow performance, short battery life, and outdated radios are the biggest detractors. If you need a bare-bones tablet with a large display and expandable storage, it might make sense, but most people should consider the Lenovo IdeaTab Plus for its lower price and better all-around performance instead. I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: SALES: 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house. Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more. Top picks: FAQ: What are the best brands for travel slippers? Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home. Should you wear slippers on a plane? Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom. What should you look for in the best indoor slippers? When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: REVIEW: Sennheiser keeps the Momentum going with great improvements over the True Wireless 4
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central
There’s a lot to talk about with the Momentum True Wireless 5, because they're an upgrade compared to the Momentum TW 4 in almost every way that matters. From sound quality to ANC and quality-of-life improvements, if you prioritize sound over ANC, Sennheiser’s latest is worth serious consideration. Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Sennheiser is one of my go-to audio brands for quality consumer and reference audio. And for good reason: they often produce products that have crystal clarity, are well-balanced with great detail retrieval, while still being fun to listen to rather than clinical. When it comes to their Bluetooth devices, they prioritize audio quality over active noise canceling, but with the introduction of their new Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5, they’re closer than ever to ANC market leaders Sony and Bose. While I love Sennheiser’s sound quality, their boxy Bluetooth earbuds have not been the stuff of aesthetic excellence. I’ve never called previous models “ugly,” but their looks have been rather dull. The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 (Momentum TW5 from here on) look like an artisan took the TW4 and carved away the boxy shape, smoothing those angular edges into a sleek, aerodynamic aesthetic (see the photo comparison in the gallery above). This year, I have the Copper colorway, which is a combination of beautiful copper earbuds and case trim with textured brown case exteriors and the signature Sennheiser logo in copper on the ‘buds and silver on the case top. The case fits much better in my pants’ coin pocket this year than last year. Gone is the small, boxy case. Instead, you get a slim, pocketable case with wired and wireless charging, plus other features I’ll touch on shortly. The earbuds from the previous generation fit my ears well, thanks to their shape and the silicone wings around the edges. The wings are gone now, but with the new shape and ergonomics, they fit my ears just as well as they did before, and that’s despite actually being heavier than the Momentum TW4, which also feels bulkier in my ears compared to the new Momentum TW5. Though the aesthetic upgrade is definitely welcome, the most important upgrades for many people will likely be the audio improvements in both sound reproduction and active noise canceling. Let’s talk ANC, first. During my day one testing, I realized I’d need to pull out my previously tested Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds because my first listen had me wondering whether Sennheiser had upped their ANC game to those levels; it was that good! When it comes to noise-canceling earbuds, you can focus on either sound quality or aggressive noise canceling. Prioritizing one often comes at the expense of the other, so while Sennheiser’s ANC on previous models was good, it wasn’t market-leading. This time, Sennheiser’s engineers have greatly improved ANC across the frequency spectrum. Though I wouldn’t run out to upgrade my earbuds just for improved ANC, this year’s model is definitely more aggressive at canceling noise than the Momentum TW4. You’ll hear more complete cancellation across the frequency spectrum. That means that you’ll hear less high-pitched urban traffic noise or subway sounds. Keyboard keystrokes should be a bit quieter. Cars whizzing by you; their engine noises will have decreased compared to the previous generation. And while that's true when you compare the Momentum TW5 to the TW4, Sony’s WF-1000XM6 still hushes more of those same frequencies than the TW5. The difference in 2026 is that Sennheiser has closed the distance between the ANC it offers and what you’ll get from Sony. While the durability hasn’t changed, the Momentum TW5 carries the same IP54 rating as the previous generation; Sennheiser has upgraded the longevity of this year’s model with user-replaceable batteries in both the earbuds and the charging case. On the charging case, that upgrade is pretty clear if you look at the single Philips head screw on the bottom right side of the case, across from the oddly placed USB-C charging port on the left. I’m guessing that port placement is the result of making the battery removable. The Momentum TW5 comes with a prying tool to remove the battery, but you’ll need to provide the Philips PH000 screwdriver. This is a Phillips head (the “star”) screwdriver with a 7mm blade. Sennheiser lists the battery part number as BA 501, but it isn’t listed for sale on their site yet. I thoroughly enjoy Sennheiser’s sound signature. I use their IE900 IEMs as reference in-ear headphones, and their HD660S as one of my over-ear reference audio headphones, along with pairs from Dali and Fosi. The Momentum TW5 expands sound quality across the frequency range, with its signature focus on the mid-range to deliver great instrument separation and strong vocal presentation without sacrificing low-end energy. Listening to Charles Mingus’ “Moanin’,” the TW5 does a much better job than the Sony WF-1000XM6 at maintaining a strong sense of instrumentation during the song's most frenetic parts. Where Sony turns those sections into a pot of mashed potatoes, Sennheiser allows you to continue to hear where the sound of different instruments comes from in the stereo image. Listening to various folk songs, including Paul Simon’s “Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes,” where his voice can get sibilant with audio products that have harsher, or overly energetic high-frequency reproduction, the TW5 were smooth. No sibilance from Simon, and no eardrum-fatiguing high notes from Joni Mitchell’s “River (With French Horns) [Blue Sessions].” Around the minute mark on Mitchell’s song, she hits some sustained high notes that drive me batty on clinical headphones or those with poor high-frequency reproduction, but again, the TW5 are more on the smooth end of the spectrum. If you listen and disagree with my assessment, the good news is that this year the Sennheiser Smart Control+ app has expanded its five-band EQ to eight bands, so you’ll have more control over shaping the sound to your preferences, and the pair of buds take well to EQ adjustments. My only real issue with the TW5 was the microphones when making phone calls. They sound excellent indoors, but outdoors, they'll block noise superbly, but at the cost of audio stability. At times, when the AI is working hard to block background noise, I've found that audio quality can take a hit. Overall, you'll sound great, and so will the folks calling you, but be aware that, depending on ambient noise, you may experience some finicky behavior. In terms of battery life, I've found that I can get a day's use out of them with ANC off. For me, that's around 10 hours, including a trip to my local climbing gym. ANC on has given less, though a little better than some competitors, getting a little over six hours in my testing. More bass-heavy tracks in your rotation will affect that, though. In the final analysis, you have Bluetooth earbuds that folks love for various reasons. Some lock you into an ecosystem and are superior in part because of how they work inside that walled garden, while others are more open and fully stand on their own. The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are the latter, and while they aren’t market leaders in ANC or calling, they’re solid performers in those areas and offer a delightfully entertaining, engaging sound signature that you’ll get extra years out of, thanks to their user-serviceable batteries. Smart, effective upgrades! Sennheiser gives consumers a worthy upgrade over the Momentum True Wireless 5. They've improved the sound and noise-cancelling quality, made the batteries removable in both the buds and the case, and refined the exterior. A worthy upgrade!

item.title: REVIEW: OneRep review: A simple way to erase your personal information online
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- Automates data-broker removal requests - Broad coverage of public and non-public data brokers - Clear dashboard for tracking removal progress - Some discovered profiles couldn’t be independently inspected - Past ties to the data-broker industry may raise trust concerns OneRep simplifies the process of removing personal information from data-broker sites, with a straightforward dashboard and easy tracking. It’s a worthwhile option for anyone who values convenience over the cost of doing the work themselves. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined You don’t have to share much personal information online for it to end up in the hands of data brokers. These companies gather information from public records and other sources, compiling it into searchable profiles that can reveal your home address, phone number, and even the names of your relatives. Tracking down and removing that information yourself is tedious, especially when dozens of sites may have your details. OneRep promises to make the job easier by finding your information and handling removal requests on your behalf. I tested the service against my own digital footprint to see how much work it could save me—and whether it could actually make my information disappear. OneRep searches data-broker sites for your personal information, submits removal requests on your behalf, and follows up when brokers don’t respond or comply. The service works with two types of data brokers. Public brokers, commonly called people-search sites, make personal profiles available online. OneRep scans these sites for matching records and requests their removal. Non-public brokers, meanwhile, share personal information with advertisers and other businesses without making it openly searchable. Because OneRep can’t inspect their records directly, it sends opt-out requests to these companies after obtaining your consent. Removing a profile doesn’t necessarily mean it’s gone for good. Scrubbing your data from these sites can feel like bailing water out of a leaky boat because data brokers continually collect fresh information and can recreate deleted profiles. To address this, OneRep rescans covered people-search sites monthly and submits new removal requests when records reappear. OneRep offers four subscription plans. Individual coverage costs $14.95 per month or $8.33 per month with annual billing. Family coverage for up to six people costs $27.95 monthly or $15 per month annually. Both plans cover 317 public people-search sites. The Individual Pro and Family Pro plans expand coverage to 876 brokers, including 559 non-public ones. They cost $29.95 and $55.95 per month, respectively, or $15.95 and $29.95 per month with annual billing. Pro subscribers also get expert assistance and unlimited custom removal requests for brokers outside OneRep’s automated coverage. Those requests must involve data brokers, however. OneRep won’t remove information from government records, news websites, or social media platforms. You can run a free scan to see where your personal information appears before subscribing. OneRep also offers a five-day free trial of its removal service, though you’ll need to provide payment information and cancel before the trial ends to avoid being charged. Because OneRep requires access to sensitive personal information, the company’s own privacy practices are worth considering. The company has faced scrutiny over its ties to the data-broker industry. In 2024, security journalist Brian Krebs reported that founder Dimitri Shelest had created numerous people-search businesses. Shelest acknowledged retaining an ownership stake in Nuwber, a data broker. The revelations prompted Mozilla to announce it was ending its partnership with OneRep. A OneRep representative told me that Nuwber has since shut down and Shelest no longer holds an ownership stake in any data broker or people-search business. The company maintains that it has never shared customer information with those businesses. OneRep announced that it completed a SOC 2 Type II audit in 2025, which assessed its security and confidentiality controls over time. To start using OneRep, you have to enter your name, date of birth, and contact information. You can also add previous addresses, alternate names, and additional phone numbers or email addresses. It sounds counterintuitive to hand a service the same information you’re asking it to remove, but providing enough details helps distinguish your records from those of people with the same or similar names. The dashboard gives you a running picture of OneRep’s progress. At the top, a summary shows how many profiles OneRep has discovered, how many removals are underway, and how many have been completed. It also displays your overall removal percentage and an estimate of the time you would have spent removing the records yourself. Another section shows how many sites OneRep has scanned and how many contain profiles matching your information. Further down, you can examine the findings broker by broker. Each entry identifies the personal information OneRep discovered, along with the current removal status and estimated processing time. You can also follow links to view the exposed profile, open a sample report showing the types of information a broker collects, or get instructions for removing the record yourself. OneRep requires separate authorization before contacting non-public brokers. You’ll need to agree to share identifying information, potentially including your date of birth, so these companies can locate your records. OneRep also creates a temporary email address to handle their responses without exposing your personal email address. Once I gave my consent, the dashboard showed requests processing across 559 non-public brokers. OneRep’s initial scan turned up 47 profiles containing my personal information across 39 people-search sites. Along with current and former addresses, the records included phone numbers, email addresses, and names of relatives. Some of the information was outdated, but much of it was accurate. One Spokeo listing was particularly revealing. The profile appeared to belong to my deceased father, who shared my name, and listed his age rather than mine. But it also contained my phone number and email address, along with several addresses where I’d lived. One was my childhood home, which I hadn’t lived in since 1990. The mixed-up profile illustrated how data brokers can combine information about different people into a single record, potentially exposing someone’s contact information and address history to people searching for someone else. OneRep lets you inspect the records it finds, though the links weren’t always helpful. The Spokeo link opened the actual profile, while a link to BeenVerified took me to its homepage. From there, I had to go through the site’s regular search process, which eventually asked me to pay to view the report. I declined, so I couldn’t independently check the information OneRep had found. Once my removal requests started processing, I checked the dashboard periodically for updates. After a week, OneRep reported that it had removed six of the 47 profiles, with the remaining 41 still in progress. By day 12, that number had climbed to 21 removals, or 45 percent of the total records found. That was encouraging progress, given that OneRep’s estimated removal times ranged from days to months. I checked two of those completed removals myself. Clicking the removal link for National Public Data opened a page confirming that the record had been removed. PeopleWin presented a less definitive result: A search for my name still returned nine profiles, but none belonged to me. Both findings were consistent with OneRep’s reported results, though the National Public Data confirmation was more convincing. The outstanding requests weren’t necessarily a cause for concern. Each broker has its own removal procedures and response times, and OneRep may need to make repeated attempts before a record disappears. Data removal is a long game, and I’ll need to keep an eye on the dashboard over the coming weeks to see how many more removals the service completes. OneRep also includes data breach monitoring, which identified 23 incidents associated with my primary email address. The feature draws on the data breach tracking service Have I Been Pwned and provides details about each exposure, including what information was compromised. Clicking through to the recommendations brought me to OneRep articles offering general security advice rather than guidance tailored to the individual incident. It’s a convenient addition to OneRep’s dashboard, though you can get much of the same information and free breach alerts directly from Have I Been Pwned. Is OneRep worth it? OneRep is a good choice for anyone who wants to reduce their online exposure without handling dozens of opt-out requests themselves. My early results were encouraging, though I’d want to see how many more removals OneRep completes before judging its long-term effectiveness. The subscription cost is worth considering, particularly since keeping your information off data-broker sites may require ongoing monitoring and payments. Whether that expense is justified largely comes down to how much time and effort you’re willing to spend protecting your privacy. If you’re comfortable handling opt-outs yourself, you can save money by using free removal tools and following brokers’ instructions. But if you’d rather leave the work to someone else, OneRep offers a convenient alternative. I’d recommend starting with the standard Individual plan unless you specifically need Pro’s expanded broker coverage.

item.title: REVIEW: Samsung P9 USB4 portable SSD review: 4GB/s speeds that hold up on long transfers
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
If you're a video editor, photographer, or other power user that needs ultra-fast portable storage, the options are relatively limited. Samsung's latest P9 USB4 External Solid-State Drive changes that, though, with up to 4,000MB/s transfer rates. I've spent the past few weeks with this tiny-but-mighty portable drive, and it has made it easier for me to edit photos and videos both at home and on the go. Though expensive at $650 for the 2TB model, I think this drive is absolutely worth it if you need internal drive performance from a USB SSD. - 2TB (also 1TB, 4TB, 8TB) Samsung's P9 USB4 portable solid-state drive is one of the first 4GB/s drives to hit the market. With a 40Gb/s USB4 port backing it, this compact drive delivers transfer speeds that rival internal NVMe drives, but using a portable USB-C cable design instead of requiring an internal M.2 mount. - Holds strong speeds on long sustained writes - Compact metal design with a 6.5-foot drop rating - Expensive, especially at higher capacities - Needs a full 40Gbps USB4 port for full speed The Samsung P9 USB4 External SSD comes in four sizes ranging from 1TB to 8TB with pricing starting at $340. It is available to purchase at Amazon, directly from Samsung, and B&H Photo Video. - 6.5-foot drop resistance, no IP rating - 3.39 oz (96g) Twice the T9's speed, if your port can keep up I have used many "fast" portable drives. PNY's Duo Link V3 is my favorite flash drive that I've ever used—it's fast and compact with around 1GB/s transfer speeds. Crucial's X10 portable SSD was one of the first portable drives that I used which started to feel more like internal storage than just something plugged into my computer. The previous-generation Samsung T9 could even hit 2GB/s transfer rates. The Samsung P9 takes portable drives to a whole new level that I've never experienced before. With transfer speeds rated at 4,000MB/s read and 3,800MB/s write (4GB/s and 3.8GB/s), I was quite skeptical going into this review that I would actually hit those speeds. However, with the right cable and computer, it is entirely possible to move data faster than a PCIe 3.0 NVMe drive over a USB cable. On my M1 Max MacBook Pro, I saw transfer speeds of 3,450MB/s read and 3,163MB/s write in AmorphousDiskMark. On Windows, using DiskSpd, I saw transfer speeds of 4,066MB/s read and 3,265MB/s write. While I didn't quite hit the 3,800MB/s write speeds that Samsung claims, I still got pretty close to what it showed and even overshot the read speeds by a hair. Normally, I expect to come in under what a manufacturer claims for transfer rates as they always report "ideal conditions" and testing in the real-world is never ideal. This drive holds up well with long writes Barely noticeable slowdowns only show up after hundreds of gigabytes Those numbers above are just benchmark numbers, though. Whenever I tested the drive with real-world file transfers, it felt just as fast. I moved around 1.8TB of data from my MacBook to my desktop when I moved from macOS to Windows a few weeks ago and it only took about 20 minutes to transfer all the files. When doing small file transfers, I definitely saw the 4,000MB/s read and 3,000MB/s+ write speeds. But, during longer sustained writes, transfer speeds definitely fell some. Rates didn't drop to abysmal speeds—it actually held up at about 1,800MB/s for me when I was writing several hundred gigabytes at a time. This lines up with what Samsung rates the drive at. After TurboWrite (the caching system of the drive) is full, it should sit at around 2,000MB/s transfer speeds. I did see a little bit of a further drop off after around 250GB was transferred, with speeds falling to around 1,655MB/s, but that's honestly not bad at all for an external drive like this. Overall, this is the absolute fastest external drive that I have used and one of the fastest on the market. Samsung is definitely showing its strength here. Plug it into the wrong port and all the benefits go out the window Your 10Gb/s ports cut it to old-drive speeds This should go without saying, but I'll say it anyway: you need a full 40Gb/s USB4 port to take full advantage of this drive. If it gets plugged into a 10Gb/s port, you'll lose 75% of the speed the drive has to offer. Same with a 20Gb/s port—you'll lose 50% of the speed. The thing is, not all USB4 ports are created equal. I have a Strix Halo desktop that has USB4 on the front of it and it refuses to see this drive at USB4 speeds. My MacBook Pro and Lenovo Yoga Mini PC both see it at 40Gb/s speeds (using the same cable). That port seems finicky though, as it works with other USB4 devices just fine at the full 40Gb/s bandwidth. But, it does go to show that USB4 is a very finicky standard. I still remember when USB 3.0 came out and people fell back to using USB 2.0 when installing an operating system because it was more reliable—this feels like that. It's not Samsung's fault—the drive works exactly how it should in multiple computers. But, it's definitely worth noting that if you don't plug it into a compatible port, it will slow down. Thankfully, the drive supports USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 which is 20Gb/s, USB 3.2 Gen 2 10Gb/s, and USB 3.2 Gen 1 5Gb/s. So, you'll get the fastest transfer speeds possible of whatever port you plug it into. This drive is rugged enough to handle just about anything you throw at it I don't know about you, but my technology has to withstand quite the beating. Outside of my laptop and iPad, I really just toss stuff in my laptop bag and say, "Good luck!" The P9 has withstood everything that I've put it through. Not only can it stand up to daily wear and tear, but it actually is rated for a 6.5-foot drop and the shock that goes along with it, as well as being able to withstand running in hotter environments. Under load in my office, it never got above 37°C and that was after writing 1TB of data consistently. One thing I wish Samsung would have added here is some form of IP rating to protect it from water intrusion. Even a low rating, like IP54 would have been nice to see. As it is, the only "durability" that Samsung gives the drive is a 6.5-foot fall resistance. Should you buy the Samsung P9 USB4 External SSD? Realistically, I think there are very few reasons that one would need 4GB/s transfer speeds on an external SSD. However, if you do need to move data that fast, then Samsung's P9 is one of the best options out there, even at $650 for the 2TB version. The thing is, building a DIY NVMe enclosure that could get anywhere close to the read/write speeds of the Samsung P9 will set you back around $460, if not more (depending on the drive you choose). The P9 is an all-in-one system that's plug-and-play, and there's a lot to be said for that. At the end of the day, I think the Samsung P9 USB4 external SSD is a fantastic piece of expensive tech that lives up to the hype if you need blazing-fast read and write speeds on the go. It has become my new go-to portable drive for on-the-go photo and video editing, and I absolutely love it.

item.title: REVIEW: Eney, the Mac AI Assistant That Actually Gets Things Done
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
We all know the familiar pattern of settling in for a focused work session. You sit down with a hot cup of coffee, ready to dive in, only to watch digital clutter instantly hijack your focus. Half an hour vanishes as you bounce between news tabs, hunt down buried downloads, and piece together messy email threads. Traditional web chatbots promised to solve this daily friction, but they often add more steps by forcing you to constantly copy, paste, and reformat text in a browser window. To eliminate this frustration, the team at MacPaw created Eney. Known for polished apps like CleanMyMac and Setapp, they built Eney as a truly action-oriented assistant designed exclusively for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS. Instead of living in another generic web browser tab, it runs directly on your desktop, coordinating with native apps to automate tedious chores so you can stay in the flow. Putting Eney through its paces over a typical workday quickly showed me how different it feels from other AI tools. Streamlining the Morning Routine with One Click Getting started with Eney required virtually no setup. You can completely skip prompt engineering tutorials and complex scripts because the application arrives ready to handle your daily desktop routine right out of the box. My first test focused on streamlining my morning routine. Rather than falling down an endless rabbit hole of browser tabs, I turned to the built-in news workflow. Eney scanned the web, gathered top stories across tech and current events, and presented a clean, digestible summary right on screen. Getting a five-story overview in under a minute kept my workspace clutter-free and my mind clear. Real Task Execution and Honest System Boundaries Where Eney really shone was during hands-on task execution. When I needed to send a quick project update about an upcoming article, I asked Eney to draft the message. It generated a polished draft tailored to my brief. Best of all, it offered total peace of mind by explicitly confirming that the text remained a draft and would never be sent without my direct approval. The app handles end-of-day handoffs just as seamlessly. Testing the evening briefing feature showed how naturally it helps you wind down. When it is time to wrap up, Eney reviews your calendar and tasks, highlights completed items, previews the upcoming day, and gives you a satisfying sense of closure before you log off. Another thing that made this experience feel utterly reliable was how transparently Eney respects macOS privacy settings. When I chose not to give it access to my inbox, the app clearly explained that it could not review messages without Full Disk Access. It never pretends to work around permissions, keeping sensitive personal data fully under your control. Working In Place with Web Summaries and Eney Wand Sifting through dense articles or technical pages can drain your energy fast when you only need a handful of takeaways. I ran into that exact friction during research, which turned out to be the perfect opportunity to test the floating Eney Wand. When you highlight a passage on an open page, the Wand immediately surfaces alongside your selection with smart shortcuts to translate text, set up a calendar event, or summarize the material. Moreover, without needing to copy chunks of text into a separate browser window, you can just ask it to break down the article right where you are reading. Eney scans the active page, strips away the clutter, and delivers the key points in clean bullet points directly over your screen. Why not give Eney a spin? Anyone wanting to cut down on daily administrative busywork will love how naturally Eney weaves into a macOS workflow to protect focus. Trying the app comes with zero risk. You can seamlessly download Eney and evaluate it for 14 days or up to 10,000 credits, whichever comes first. The trial requires no payment info or credit card, so you can explore everything on your actual workload before spending a dime. When you are ready for full access, MacPaw offers three simple monthly tiers. The Starter tier comes for $14.99 per month for 10,000 credits. The Boost tier costs $29.99 per month for 20,000 credits and the Power tier costs $49.99 per month for 30,000 credits. All plans renew monthly and can be canceled at any time. Standard pricing includes applicable taxes and is processed in US dollars, with final costs depending on your bank’s conversion rate. If you ever hit your limit during a busy month, top-up credits are available on demand. Added to that, the unused monthly credits don’t roll over, and you can choose the tier that fits your regular habits. So, put it to test for 14 days and find out how much lighter your workday feels once your Mac takes the wheel.

item.title: REVIEW: After 8 days with Apple’s first smart display, I’m convinced HomeView was worth the wait
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Apple's first smart display is a strong start. The HomeView combines a beautiful design, surprisingly powerful sound, thoughtful personalization, and a much smarter Siri into a device that fits naturally into everyday life. It's not perfect — third-party app support is limited, and some Siri requests still take longer than I'd like — but after eight days living with two HomeViews, I've found plenty to love. Most importantly, it's useful when I need it, and happily fades into the background when I don't. - +Modern, thoughtful design with excellent clock faces - +Excellent sound quality from the tabletop model - +Personalized experiences and genuinely useful Siri AI - +Seamless smart-home controls and FaceTime - -Requires an iPhone to set up, with newer models needed for the full experience - -Siri can be slow to respond to some requests Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Apple's first smart display is a strong start, even if it's a somewhat strange first-generation product. The HomeView gets a lot right, from its distinctly Apple design and excellent audio to its personalized experience and genuinely useful Siri AI capabilities. And after eight days of living with two HomeViews, I really like what Apple has delivered. First and foremost, though, the HomeView is for folks already invested in the Apple ecosystem. You'll need an iPhone to get the most out of it, and ideally an Apple Intelligence-enabled model to take full advantage of Siri AI and Personal Context. This integration is what makes the HomeView special, letting Siri find information in your messages, control your smart home, and surface personal content without you constantly having to reach for your phone. The hardware is excellent, with a compact, premium design and a vibrant 7-inch display. I've been using the speaker-mounted 'countertop' HomeView in my kitchen, and the wall-mounted version in my entryway, and both fit naturally into my daily routine. I especially love the Photos clock face, which intelligently cycles through pictures of my dog Rosie, family, and friends. Audio is another standout. The standard HomeView delivers surprisingly powerful bass, a wide soundstage, and enough volume to fill my kitchen and living room. Music support is so strong that I've actually been occasionally using it as my main speaker. Siri AI is impressive, too, particularly when tapping into Personal Context, though it's not always the fastest. Simple smart-home requests are generally quick, while more complex tasks can take 10 to 15 seconds. Still, the ability to ask Siri to find a song a friend recommended in my messages and then play it is pretty neat. There are some limitations, though. There's no App Store at launch, third-party apps are restricted, and video options are limited. While I'd have liked to see more flexibility, I suspect Apple's curated approach is intentional. HomeView feels designed to be a more mindful, ambient device that surfaces information when you need it rather than another screen constantly demanding your attention. That being said, I wouldn’t be shocked if, when WWDC 27 rolls around, a dedicated 'home' OS is announced, and the app experience opens up. At $299 / £299 / AU$449, the HomeView certainly isn't cheap, but it also doesn't feel like an unfinished first-generation experiment. It's already great for FaceTime calls, quickly checking messages, playing music, controlling smart home devices, and displaying personalized clock faces. These are the kinds of everyday interactions that make it easy to appreciate having the HomeView around, rather than feeling like you're searching for reasons to use it. Ultimately, the Apple HomeView feels like a natural companion to your iPhone, giving you a reason to leave it in your pocket rather than constantly reaching for it. It's a smart-home controller, digital photo frame, surprisingly capable speaker, and personal assistant rolled into one, but it's also perfectly happy just showing you the time or a favorite photo. It's not perfect, but Apple has delivered a thoughtful, genuinely useful first-generation product that feels like a very strong start, especially if you're already deep in its ecosystem. - Premium, distinctly Apple design with a vibrant 7-inch Liquid Retina display - Two designs: tabletop and wall-mounted, with the same core features The HomeView comes in two distinct styles: standard and wall-mounted. The standard HomeView will likely be the more popular option, and features a square 7-inch Liquid Retina display with soft, rounded corners that sits on an arm extending from a domed, circular base. It's smaller than you might expect, and pretty cute. It comes in four colors: Starlight, Space Gray, Rose Pink, and Silver. I've been testing Starlight, which looks like an airy gold or more silver depending on how the light hits it. Apple also includes a color-matched USB-C cable and wall adapter, making physical setup straightforward. The design is distinctly Apple, with a premium aluminum build combining brushed finishes and polished accents, particularly around the hinge connecting the display to the base. At first glance, it's almost like an oversized Apple Watch — perhaps an earlier generation thanks to the fairly thick bezels. There's also a bit of the iconic, potted-plant-like iMac G4 in its DNA, and I quite like that. The display can tilt up or down, but not left or right. For that, you'll need to manually turn the entire HomeView, though the rubberized bottom, similar to a HomePod or HomePod mini, keeps it firmly planted. And while it’s easy enough to turn it left or right with the display, a swivel mechanism built in here would have made this more seamless. I've been testing the standard HomeView in my apartment, where the kitchen flows right into the living space, and I've found a natural home for it on my kitchen island. Thanks to its compact size, I can easily slide it around or turn it to face wherever I am, whether I'm making coffee, cooking dinner, or hopping on a FaceTime call. Center Stage does a good job of keeping me in frame, but it can only follow me so far before I need to turn the display manually. A motorized arm would be pretty dope, and I'm holding out hope for one in a future generation. The 7-inch Liquid Retina display looks great, with clear text, vibrant photos, and plenty of brightness, though its glossy finish can still catch reflections even when the brightness is cranked up, and I would be surprised if Nano-Texture or a similar coating might be ushered in a future generation. Apple says it can dim down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest of any display in its lineup, which is likely handy for bedrooms and helps ensure it’s not glowing in the middle of the night or in dimmer conditions. It's excellent for displaying photos, album artwork, or lyrics in Apple Music, and I've never had an issue reading text. It's also noticeably thicker than an iPad or even Apple's now touch-enabled MacBook Pro, though that's understandable given everything packed inside. Above the display sits a 12-megapixel Ultra Wide camera, while tiny microphone openings are dotted around the frame, including near the camera, along the sides, and on the rear. You won't find any physical buttons or a camera shutter, though, as Apple is betting almost entirely on touch and voice. The only port is USB-C for power. The base is where much of the audio hardware lives, with dozens of precisely drilled holes around its lower half. There are two full-range drivers built into the display section, while the base houses a downward-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators. I'll dig deeper into sound quality below, but it's surprisingly robust for something this small, with plenty of low-end punch without causing HomeView to vibrate excessively or topple over. Overall, HomeView feels a good bit more premium than older Echo smart displays or Google's Nest Hub, though it takes a markedly different approach from Amazon's newer Echo Show 8, 11, and forthcoming Echo Show 16. It fits neatly into Apple's broader design ethos, even if the colors, somewhat ironically, don't necessarily match those of the HomePod or HomePod mini. I've also been testing the second version, which Apple calls HomeView (Wall Mounted). While the standard model is more versatile, there's a lot to like about having Apple's smart display permanently positioned on a wall. Unboxing is considerably simpler, as you're essentially getting just the display, without the arm or speaker base. On the back is a USB-C port, which is designed to work with compatible mounts, including those from Schneider Electric, which were developed specifically for HomeView. Importantly, you're not sacrificing the core experience. The wall-mounted version has the same processor, display, cameras, sensors, and software as the tabletop model. The biggest hardware difference is audio, handled by two custom drivers rather than the more elaborate speaker system in the standard HomeView. It's by no means tinny and still offers a surprisingly wide soundstage, but there's less oomph, particularly in the low end. I suspect most folks opting for the wall-mounted model will want to wire it directly into the wall for the cleanest possible look. But as a renter, I went with Schneider Electric's USB-C wall mount, and it was one of the simplest mounting experiences I've had with a smart home device. Two drilled holes, anchors, screws, and probably less than 15 minutes later, it was on the wall. From there, I connected the lengthy USB-C cable to a power adapter, which you'll need to supply yourself. I've been using the wall-mounted HomeView in my entryway, and it's a great fit. Walking in to see photos of my pup Rosie, my nieces, or family and friends is a lovely touch, while the customizable Smart Home face turns it into a central control panel. I'll dig into that experience, including some surprisingly useful features, more below. Ultimately, the standard HomeView likely offers better overall value thanks to its more powerful audio system and flexibility to move between rooms. But the wall-mounted version feels especially well suited to an entryway, kitchen, or another central location where you want information and smart home controls available at a glance. Both feel thoughtfully designed, and Apple has delivered two distinct approaches to what a smart home display can look like. - Siri AI and Personal Context deliver genuinely useful, personalized experiences - Excellent sound quality, responsive smart home controls, and impressive FaceTime performance - Limited third-party apps and streaming options, and complex Siri requests can be slow I've been living with two HomeViews for eight days, with one serving me well on the entryway wall of my apartment, and the other primarily living in my kitchen. The standard model has also spent some time in my office and even the bedroom, and I've been putting both through their paces. HomeView is built around your iPhone, and that tight integration is central to the experience. You'll also want an Apple Intelligence-enabled model to get the most out of Siri AI and Personal Context. Thankfully, it all works quite well. I've used HomeView for everything from music and FaceTime calls to smart home controls, checking messages, and displaying photos. I've even watched some Apple TV, though it's hardly the ideal screen for that. Setup feels familiar if you've ever paired an Apple Watch or AirPods with an iPhone. Plug HomeView in, wait for it to boot up and say hello, then bring your iPhone nearby. From there, you scan a graphic to pair the devices and follow a few steps, including choosing who you're setting it up for. HomeView is designed to be communal, sitting in a shared space where multiple people can use it, but also personal when the situation calls for it. It supports up to six registered users, and adding someone starts on HomeView before handing the process over to their iPhone. They'll also need to be part of your Apple Home. The personalization works particularly well. For instance, while I was viewing my messages, my dad walked into the camera's view, and HomeView immediately stopped showing my personal content until it could recognize me again. It's a clever safeguard, especially for a device that's meant to live in a shared space. It does mean, though, that some items you’d think would be shared among users are missing. For example, there's no calendar — likely because it might contain confidential items, and Apple wants to make sure those are shown to a registered user. But that does mean the HomeView doesn’t offer a shared calendar like, say a Skylight or an Echo. One solution would be a shared calendar that is shared with each person (up to six) who is registered on the HomeView. The HomeView runs custom software, not HomeViewOS, that borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The app grid, including its tint and customizable widgets, feels like iOS, while customizing the clock faces is more akin to watchOS, complete with complications. It's a bit of a Frankenstein-like approach, but it works. And speaking of clock faces, they're one of my favorite parts of HomeView. Snoopy is especially delightful, with custom-designed artwork and animations separate from what you'll find on Apple TV. You can even tap Snoopy to trigger an animation, which is an adorable little touch. The Photos face is equally impressive, and really shows how personal HomeView can feel. You can select people, places, or pets, and HomeView will intelligently surface and cycle through relevant photos. I chose my dog Rosie during setup, and I love seeing different photos of her throughout the day. You can even tap the screen to see when and where a particular photo was taken. I could easily see HomeView being a great gift for parents or family members for this feature alone, especially since you can use a shared photo album as the source and have new photos appear as they're added. It turns what could have been a pretty ordinary clock face into something much more personal. There's also the Modular face, which lets you customize the display with widgets and complications, putting useful information and controls front and center. Between that, Photos, and Snoopy, Apple has done an excellent job making the clock faces feel like more than just a way to tell the time. In terms of responsiveness, HomeView generally feels quite snappy. Apple's A18 chip is under the hood, complete with the Secure Enclave, which plays an important role in the device's privacy protections. Apple handles processing on-device when possible, while more complex requests can be handled through Private Cloud Compute. You'll still need your iPhone for the more personalized experiences, though, as HomeView draws on the content and apps connected to your device. And that's what enables some of its most impressive tricks. For instance, I asked Siri which Dave Matthews Band song my friend Benjie wanted me hear. HomeView took a moment to think — probably around 10 to 15 seconds — while displaying updates at the top of the screen as it searched through my messages. It eventually came back with the answer: "Ants Marching." I then asked Siri to play it, and since I have both Spotify and Nugs connected through my iPhone, it asked which service I wanted to use before starting playback. It's an impressive interaction, even if Siri takes its time, and I appreciate seeing updates on what it's working on. I could also ask Siri to look at my calendar, find an event in the city, and figure out when I need to leave based on traffic. It's another multi-step request that isn't instantaneous, but it gets me to the answer. Response times can vary quite a bit, though. When I asked Siri to play Ghosts by Bruce Springsteen, it took about 12 seconds before the song started playing through Apple Music, complete with album artwork on the display. A simpler request, like checking the weather in New York City, took closer to two or three seconds. Smart home requests, thankfully, are considerably quicker. Asking Siri for the temperature in my apartment, pulling data from both HomeViews, multiple sensors, and my Nest thermostat, takes about two seconds, if not less. I can also quickly turn on my Philips Hue lights or adjust the temperature, and those everyday interactions have worked well. Of course, you don't have to rely on Siri to control your smart home. The HomeView has a dedicated Home app that's similar to what you'll find on your iPhone or iPad, but it's the Home Modular clock face that really turns it into a smart home control panel, especially when wall-mounted. You can customize it with blocks showing key information, like the temperature or readings from connected sensors, alongside easy touch controls for lights, thermostats, and other smart home devices. Everything is in one place, and I've found it especially useful on the HomeView in my entryway, where I can quickly see what's happening around my apartment or make an adjustment without reaching for my iPhone. You'll also find automations you've previously created in the Home app, but the HomeView takes things a step further by letting you create new ones simply by asking Siri. These can be single actions or more complex, multi-step routines. For instance, I asked Siri to create an automation that raises the smart blinds in my apartment and turns on the lights every morning at 6am. It handled the request, and just like that, I had a new morning routine without setting it up manually in the Home app. The broader smart home ecosystem remains somewhat confusing, particularly around compatibility. HomeView works with Apple Home and supports Matter, with Thread connectivity built in, but there's no native Zigbee support. That doesn't rule out Zigbee devices connected through a compatible bridge, though. It's worked well with my existing devices — Philips Hue lights, Google Nest Learning Thermostat 4th Gen, Eve Cam, an Anker Eufy camera, and Ryse Shades — and Apple's own Home Collection is set to arrive in December. Still, it's worth checking which devices will actually integrate before making the jump. I've also been impressed by the four integrated microphones, which reliably pick up my voice from across the room, even with music playing through a HomeView or the TV on in the background. That's particularly useful in my kitchen, where I can be making coffee or cooking dinner while asking Siri for information, controlling music, or making a FaceTime call without stopping what I'm doing. FaceTime is another highlight. The 12-megapixel camera delivers good video quality, and Center Stage does a solid job keeping me in frame as I move around the kitchen, though it can only follow me within the camera's field of view. On the wall-mounted HomeView in my entryway, I've also found myself asking Siri for directions, calendar updates, or simply what I've missed when getting home or starting the day. It's convenient to have that information available in a central location without pulling out my iPhone. There's also a surprisingly useful Mirror feature, accessible through Control Center, which uses the built-in camera to show a live view of yourself. You can switch between 1x and 2x views, and while it's not something I'd necessarily buy a HomeView for, it's a neat addition for a device mounted near the front door. I've used it for a quick look before heading out. Of course, the HomeView isn't an iPad, and Apple isn't trying to turn it into one. There's no App Store, and third-party app support is limited. Interestingly, Apple is leaning on CarPlay compatibility to bring select audio and video media apps to the HomeView. I've been able to use Spotify, Nugs, Apple Music Classical, and SiriusXM, though what's available can change depending on whom HomeView recognizes, since it pulls from that person's profile and connected iPhone. It's a curated experience, and I think that works well here. I get the sense it's meant to avoiding overwhelming you, or becoming another screen that's constantly demanding your attention. Instead, it's arguably Apple's first truly ambient device, designed to surface information when you need it and fade into the background when you don't. It doesn't even feature notifications except for Home alerts or when a call comes into your iPhone. It's both touch- and voice-enabled, and Apple's mainstay apps are here, including Music, Podcasts, Safari, FaceTime, Calendar, Messages, Home, Intercom, Weather, Find My, Reminders, Alarms, Timers, World Clock, Audiobooks, Apple TV, and Settings. News is also part of the experience, though the selection is still more limited than what you'd find on an iPhone or iPad. Although the HomeView has Apple TV built in, don't expect it to replace your television or even an iPad. There are no dedicated apps for YouTube, Disney+, Hulu, Peacock, or Netflix, though you can start a YouTube video on your iPhone and bring it close to your HomeView to hand off playback. And with a seven-inch display, substantial black bars, or a zoomed-in picture that crops the action, it's better suited to casual viewing while doing something else than settling in for a full TV episode or movie. Audio is another major strength, particularly on the standard HomeView. For something so compact, the sound is seriously impressive, with a wide soundstage, remarkably strong bass, and enough volume to outdo the HomePod mini 2. It easily fills both my kitchen and adjoining living room with rich, robust audio, and I've actually found myself using it as my apartment's main speaker. At times, I've also grouped it with the wall-mounted HomeView for music playback across both spaces, and the experience works quite well. The tabletop model definitely has the advantage, though, with fuller sound and considerably more low-end punch. The wall-mounted version still sounds good for its size, but if music is a priority, the standard HomeView is absolutely the one I'd choose. And while the HomeView is great for controlling my smart home, playing music, following recipes while cooking — especially with multiple pre-set timers — making FaceTime calls, and plenty more, I also appreciate that it doesn't constantly demand my attention. It doesn't make me want to reach for my iPhone, either. Sometimes, I just want to glance over to check the time, see the weather, or enjoy a photo of Rosie, and that's more than enough. The HomeView is there when I need it and fades into the background when I don't, and I think that's a big part of its appeal. Apple HomeView: Pricing and Availability Apple’s HomeView is currently up for preorder at $299 in the US, £299 in the UK, and AU$449 in Australia, and will officially launch — and begin shipping — November 13, 2026. The standard HomeView, which has a base to stand on its own and comes with a wall plug, comes in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray. There’s also the HomeView (Wall-Mounted) for the same price, available in Silver or Space Gray. With that, you’ll need to get a separate wall mount made by Schneider Electric, either one that ends with a USB-C port – a good option for renters – or an AC one, which requires proper installation. Apple HomeView: Should I Buy? You've been waiting for Apple's smart display It's been a long time coming, and the HomeView checks off many of the boxes you'd expect from a smart home hub. From music playback and quick access to Siri AI to smart home controls and a digital photo frame, Apple has delivered a strong first-generation product. You want a communal screen for everyday tasks The HomeView is excellent for those quick interactions throughout the day, whether that's checking messages, making a FaceTime call, controlling your lights, or glancing at the weather. And with personalized experiences for up to six users, it feels right at home in a shared space. I spent eight days testing two Apple HomeViews in my apartment, with the standard model primarily living on my kitchen island and the wall-mounted version installed in my entryway. I also moved the standard HomeView into my office and bedroom to see how it worked in different spaces. I used both devices throughout my daily routine, testing everything from Siri AI and Personal Context to smart home controls, music playback, FaceTime calls, messages, and customizable clock faces. I connected HomeView to my existing smart home devices, including Philips Hue lights, a Nest thermostat, and smart blinds, and tested how well it handled everyday requests and more complex tasks. I also compared the HomeView to Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub smart displays, along with several speakers, including the original HomePod mini, HomePod mini 2, second-generation HomePod, Sonos Move 2, and Sonos Era 100. I paid particular attention to audio quality, responsiveness, ease of use, and how naturally HomeView fit into my daily routine — including those moments when I wasn't actively interacting with it. First reviewed November 2026.
