item.title: SALES: AI Model Comparison Tools Offer Discounts for Unified Chat Experiences
item.description:
Source: PCMag, PCWorld
Two AI platforms are offering discounted lifetime subscriptions for users seeking to compare multiple chatbot models in a single interface. AskAnyModel, a browser-based tool that aggregates 50+ AI models including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek, and Qwen Coder, is available for $31.99 (regularly $499) with code DEAL20 through November 15. PCMag reported that the service allows users to input prompts once and view side-by-side responses from selected models, with response times and token counts displayed. It also includes image generation capabilities across supported models and access to 19 premium models like GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3 Pro, along with a Gemini model featuring Google Search grounding for up to 300 weekly chats. Users can switch models mid-conversation without losing context, and the tool runs entirely in the browser without installation. Verified buyers rate it 4.6 out of 5 across 21 reviews. Meanwhile, ChatPlayground AI, which processes prompts through 20+ models including ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, is on sale for $63.20 (regularly $619) with the same code. PCWorld noted that the Unlimited subscription allows unlimited monthly messages under a fair use policy, with prompt engineering tools to refine queries and document-based image generation. The service also includes saved chat history and priority support, though it lacks internet search functionality and is limited to desktop browsers. Both services emphasize eliminating the need for multiple subscriptions by consolidating model testing into a single workspace. Users must redeem codes within 30 days, and both new and existing customers qualify for the discounts.

item.title: REVIEW: Brother MFC-J5110DW Review: A Tireless Inkjet Workhorse for Busy Small Offices
item.description:
Source: PCMag
At first glance, the Brother MFC-J5110DW INKvestment color inkjet all-in-one (AIO) printer looks essentially identical to the MFC-J5010DW, our Editors' Choice inkjet AIO for micro and busy home offices. However, it has additional paper capacity and a larger touch-screen control panel. It also adds support for PCL and BR-Script 3 (Brother's PostScript emulation) for offices that need either, and a faster first-page-out (FPO) time, which makes it much faster overall on our tests despite matching speed ratings on the two printers' spec sheets. These extras boost the list price to $359.99. They also move the printer into the overkill range for home offices, while making it a stellar choice for busy micro offices and an Editors' Choice-winning inkjet AIO for small offices and workgroups. One of the MFC-J5110DW's strongest points is its robust paper handling. For printing, it offers two 250-sheet paper drawers, plus a 100-sheet multipurpose tray, each of which can handle stacks of paper up to legal size and auto-duplex as well. The 600-sheet total capacity is easily enough to keep paper refills down to about once a week on average, even if you hit Brother's 2,500-page peak recommended monthly duty cycle every month. Keep in mind, however, that the recommendation is for printed pages. If you print mostly in duplex, that translates to 1,250 sheets of paper. For scanning, you'll find a letter-size flatbed plus a 50-sheet duplexing automatic document feeder (ADF) that can scan both sides of up to legal-size paper in a single pass. That's a tremendous time-saver versus either manual duplexing or reversing ADFs that scan one side, turn over the page, and then scan the second side separately. Single-pass duplexing also works for copying and faxing. Menu options on the 4.3-inch front panel touch screen let you copy both one-sided and two-sided originals to either one- or two-sided copies. And for both copying and faxing, you can specify whether duplex pages should be flipped on the short edge or the long edge. The printer can also scan to and print from a cloud or local email server, a USB key plugged into the USB Type-A port to the left of the touch screen, popular cloud sites (Google Drive, Evernote, OneDrive, OneNote, Dropbox, Box, and SharePoint Online), and an assortment of Brother's own cloud apps (Easy Scan to E-Mail, Scan to Mobile, Cloud Secure Print, and more). In addition, you can use menu commands to easily create customized shortcuts—giving you a second copy command defined for legal-size paper, for example, and a third one for duplexing with letter-size. Each is added to the menus, with a maximum of 64 shortcuts (including the 13 that ship with the machine) spread across eight menu screens, each with eight shortcuts. Larger offices and workgroups in a larger company may also want to take advantage of the printer's security features. Administrators can set up a secure function lock that prevents users from entering front-panel menu commands without first identifying themselves with a PIN or ID card. (To use a card, however, you have to add a third-party USB card reader.) Administrators can also define different PINs or cards to unlock different sets of features, including secure printing. One inevitable downside of highly capable paper handling is that it increases size and weight. The MFC-J5110DW weighs 37.8 pounds and measures 13.4 by 17.1 by 17.3 inches, which means you'll probably want some help moving it into place. However, the physical setup itself is standard. Load paper, then insert the cyan, yellow, magenta, and black ink cartridges. After the printer finishes the initial step of loading ink from the cartridges, the installation routine takes you through a nozzle check, prints an alignment page, waits for you to place the page on the scan bed, then scans it and aligns itself for you. If you don't have a preference or company requirement for a particular driver, you can go to Brother's website, download either the EasySetup or Full Software package to your system, and install it. However, in addition to the standard driver included in either of these downloads, Brother also offers a PCL driver and Brother's PostScript emulation (BR-Script 3). If your company standard is PCL or PostScript, or you use programs that require PostScript, you'll need to download the individual driver separately to install it. Both choices are in the Drivers section of the Downloads page. (Note that to see them, you need to choose the Show All link in that section.) For my tests, I used Ethernet to connect both the printer and our standard Windows testbed PC to a network, then downloaded and installed the package with the standard driver. If you prefer, you can connect by USB, Wi-Fi, or Wi-Fi Direct instead. Also note that the download options include Arm drivers for Windows 11, which the company says offer full support for printing and partial support for scanning. For mobile printing, the printer also supports AirPrint and Mopria, as well as both Android and iOS versions of Brother Mobile Connect. The app, which also supports scanning to mobile devices, lets you connect to the printer using either Wi-Fi Direct or by first connecting to the same network the printer is on. Brother used to say that its INKvestment printers were tank printers, because they pumped ink from the cartridges into tanks inside the printer. However, there are now two types of INKvestment printers. One kind, which Brother calls simply "INKvestment printers," still uses ink that comes in high-yield cartridges. The other kind, which Brother calls "INKvestment Tank printers," uses ink supplied in bottles that you pour into the tanks, as you do with tank printers from Canon, Epson, and HP. The general rule is that INKvestment printers that use cartridges have lower running costs than traditional cartridge printers, but higher costs than tank printers that ship ink in bottles. More important, the rule applies to the MFC-J5110DW. Ink cartridges for the printer come in three capacities and are available individually or in packs of two to four. The super-high-yield cartridges, which offer the lowest running cost, work out to 1.5 cents per mono page and 8.25 cents per standard color page, assuming you buy the black ink in the two-cartridge pack. As always, keep in mind that when comparing printer costs, it's the total cost of ownership that matters, not the running cost alone. (For details, take a look at How to Save Money on Your Next Printer.) To judge the Brother MFC-J5110DW's performance in context, I compared its test results with those of three other AIOs that include faxing: the MFC-J5010DW, the Brother MFC-L2900DW XL, and the Epson EcoTank ET-4950. The MFC-L2900DW XL mono laser printer is only slightly less expensive than the MFC-J5110DW, and it's one of our top picks for a micro to small office. The ET-4950 is an inkjet with a higher list price than the other models in the group but lower running costs. As the chart above shows, for simplex printing, the fastest in the group was the MFC-L2900DW XL, as you might expect given mono laser technology's reputation for speed. However, the MFC-J5110DW came in a fairly close second, largely due to its faster first-page-out (FPO) time. For pages 2 through 12 of our 12-page Word file, the Brother laser, at 35ppm, beat both Brother inkjets by 10ppm. For the full 12 pages, however, the laser came in at 26ppm compared with 23ppm for the MFC-J5110DW, a difference of only 4 seconds, thanks to the inkjet's 11-second head start from a faster first page. In real-world use, that short FPO time will make the MFC-J5110DW faster for text documents of only a few pages. However, the MFC-L2900DW XL will have a significant advantage overall if you print many documents that are tens of pages long or longer. The MFC-J5010DW matched the second-place MFC-J5110DW when not including the first page. However, its longer FPO time dropped it to third place for both the Word file and the full business applications suite (latter shown below). The ET-4950 was definitively the slowest overall. The printers also finished the full business applications suite, which adds color and graphics, in the same order as for the Word file. What our charts don't show is that the MFC-J5110DW color printer was 9 seconds faster than the laser mono printer overall when printing the test's PDF, Excel, and PowerPoint files, largely thanks to its shorter FPO time. For duplex printing for the full 12-page Word file, the MFC-J5110DW came in first overall, as well as for the first sheet out (pages 1 and 2) and for pages 3 through 12. So if you print mostly in duplex, it will be the fastest in the group. For photo printing, the MFC-J5110DW's average speed for printing our 4-by-6-inch photos was a relatively slow 56 seconds, largely because, unlike most inkjets, it switches to Best quality mode when set for the recommended paper we used. Text quality in our tests was close to top tier for an inkjet, making it good enough for most purposes. All of the non-italic fonts we test that you'd most likely use in business documents were easily readable at 4 points, while the one italic font cleared that bar at 5 points. Of the two heavily stylized fonts we include with thick strokes, one was easily readable at 8 points, while the other, which is harder to render well, was easily readable at 10 points. The default graphics settings delivered nicely saturated, eye-catching color on plain paper. I saw some minor banding, but only in two full-page graphics. Most fills and gradients were appropriately smooth. The printer also did an impressive job with thin lines, including a single-pixel-wide line on a black background that many printers turn into a dashed line or fail to print entirely. For photos, using Brother's BP71GLTR photo paper, the printer delivered acceptably accurate, saturated color, neutral grays for black-and-white prints, and good contrast and shadow detail, scoring at the high end of drugstore quality overall. In our water-resistance tests on plain paper, black ink smudged slightly when I gently wiped off water drops. Color inks didn't smudge, but they lost saturation when transferred to what I was wiping with. Text on plain paper stood up to a single stroke of a highlighter but smudged slightly if I went over the same text a second time. On photo paper, both color and black inks resisted smudging. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Of the four printers mentioned here, the Brother MFC-J5110DW is our favorite for a small office by enough to make it our new top pick for a small-office inkjet. However, each of the others profiled here offers something that might make it the better fit for your needs. The MFC-L2900DW XL has the fastest simplex speed for long documents, making it a tempting choice if you don't print much in duplex, don't need color, and regularly print long documents that take advantage of its speed. And as the only laser printer, it has the most water-resistant output in the group. The ET-4950, in contrast, is the slowest in the group and the most expensive, but it's also the only true tank-based printer. Its ink, supplied in bottles, offers low enough running costs that, if you print enough pages, it can easily give you a lower total cost of ownership over its lifetime than any of the other three models. As I mentioned above, the MFC-J5010DW is our Editors' Choice winner for AIO inkjet printers for micro offices. It offers almost all the same features as the MFC-J5110DW, but has a lower paper capacity and a slower FPO time in our tests, making it best reserved for somewhat lighter use. On the other hand, it's also the smaller and lighter of the two, and it costs less. The differences make it a better fit than its big brother for a smaller office—namely, a micro or home office. In contrast, the MFC-J5110DW combines three paper feeds, more than double the paper capacity of any of the others, and high speed—particularly for short documents and duplex printing. That's more than enough to earn it our Editors' Choice award for a small-office color inkjet. Most of my current work for PCMag is about printers and projectors, but I've covered a wide variety of other subjects—in more than 4,000 pieces, over more than 40 years—including both computer-related areas and others ranging from ape language experiments, to politics, to cosmology, to space colonies. I've written for PCMag.com from its start, and for PC Magazine before that, as a Contributor, then a Contributing Editor, then as the Lead Analyst for Printers, Scanners, and Projectors, and now, after a short hiatus, back to Contributing Editor. I'm pretty sure I'm the only person who worked on every "Project Printer" blockbuster PCMag ever produced, often writing 15 or more reviews for the year's big printer blowout. (I snuck in a single review one year when I was writing a book, strictly so I could keep that claim alive.) I've always worked for PCMag as a freelancer, which has freed me to take time away to write nine books, be a major contributor to four others, and write for other publications, including Wired, Computer Shopper, Projector Central, and Science Digest, where I was Computers Editor. I also wrote a computer column at one point for The Newark Star-Ledger. Although I started my career primarily as a science (mostly physics and astronomy) and science-fiction writer (published in Analog), my non-computer-related work runs the gamut from the Project Data Book for NASA's Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite (written for GE's Astro-Space Division) to the script for a video overview of a top company in the gaming industry (that would be gambling, not video games). My books include The Underground Guide to Color Printers (Addison-Wesley), Troubleshooting Your PC (Microsoft Press), and Faster, Smarter Digital Photography (Microsoft Press). Having covered a wide range of subjects, I've developed a serial expertise in many of them. The ones most relevant to my current work at PCMag.com are all imaging technologies.

item.title: SALES: The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life. Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere. It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing. Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this. And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler. Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

item.title: REVIEW: Review: Apple's M6 iMac is pricey, but it's still a good choice for a clean desk
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
The Apple Silicon iMac got its fourth refresh this month. Every other Apple Silicon Mac has found a way to move forward over the last half-decade—we’ve gotten a more Pro design for the MacBook Pro, a mini-er design for the Mac mini, and a Mac Studio that has finally made Apple admit it doesn’t want to make the Mac Pro anymore. But the Apple Silicon iMac has always been more interested in looking backward. It’s the thin, screen-on-a-stand iMac design by way of the original Bondi Blue G3 iMac. It’s a clean and pretty desktop computer, one I see all the time in small offices and on TV shows that depict small offices. We’re long past the days when it was Apple’s primary workstation computer. So I wanted to write about this new iMac from the perspective of that entry-level iMac buyer, who chooses the iMac because it’s simple and then uses it until it breaks. What does a new iMac get you if you’re stepping up from the M1 model or comparing it against an older refurbished M4 model? Without any real external updates, what makes this iMac iteration interesting? If you haven’t used an Apple Silicon-era iMac before, here’s a brief primer. The new iMac is much thinner than the older aluminum Intel models. Its front is mostly one big 24-inch screen, surrounded on all sides by a relatively thick white bezel (I still wish black were at least an option, but Apple apparently doesn’t agree). White bezel aside, it’s by far Apple’s most colorful computer. The iMacs ship with color-matched fronts, backs, stands, keyboards, mice, trackpads, and cables. Apple has tweaked the color offerings and changed the tints of each specific color a few times over the years, but the M6 iMac uses the same six color tints (plus silver) that the M4 iMac did.

item.title: SALES: Great Hydration is About More than Just Electrolytes
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Hydration comes up a lot when we talk about performance and recovery. Are you drinking enough water? Are you getting enough electrolytes? Are you tracking your fluid intake? It can be overwhelming to keep tabs of every statistic and ounce, but the hype around hydration isn’t without cause. Hydration is not only an essential component of pre-, mid- and post-workout performance. It’s an essential part of everyday life. Electrolytes are a particular point of focus among performance athletes. Electrolytes are the minerals that help maintain the balance of fluids inside and outside your body’s cells. This is a critical consideration when it comes to high-exertion workouts where you’re losing lots of fluids through sweat. The market is more saturated (pun intended) than ever with tablets, powders and pouches galore to help you optimize and maximize your electrolyte intake. But hydration doesn’t have to be as complicated as all that—and the conversation surrounding electrolytes doesn’t have to be reserved for elite athletes. It can be an everyday consideration for your morning walk, a quick out-and-back hike, or your daily commute to the office. And it all starts with a single coconut. That’s the mission behind Harmless Harvest, a California-based company championing the coconut, turning a remarkable fruit into a remarkable lineup of products. It’s new pantry-friendly coconut water contains one ingredient: 100% coconut water with no added sugar or preservatives. The simplicity of their products ladder up to the simplicity of the brand’s philosophy—that great taste, quality ingredients, and premium tasting hydration should be for everyone to enjoy. Uncomplicated hydration doesn’t have to be a statistic for you to overanalyze—it can be an intentional and enjoyable part of your everyday life. So what’s so great about a simple bottle of coconut water? Well, it’s just that: the simplicity. All on its own, coconut water delivers naturally occurring electrolytes, including potassium, to support everyday hydration. Unlike the formulated hydration drinks, tablets and powders that rely on added electrolytes, coconut water provides those muscle-supporting, fluid-balancing minerals into every bottle of Harmless Harvest coconut water naturally. Every bottle is made with a single ingredient with that naturally sweet coconut taste that’s completely delicious and refreshing. From your pantry to wherever the day takes you, Harmless Harvest’s newest coconut water makes it easier than ever to keep great-tasting hydration close at hand. With no refrigeration required, you can keep bottles at room temperature until you’re ready to enjoy. Grab a bottle on the way to yoga, before a big day on the slopes, or just on the way to work. And unlike the traditional flash pasteurization commonly used by beverage producers, Harmless Harvest’s optimized heat treatment and micro-filtration preserves the fruit’s natural sweetness and nutrients, so you’re getting everything the mighty coconut has to offer. Another question you might be asking is why is Harmless Harvest’s coconut water pink? Rather than using additives to control color variation from bottle to bottle, the company has embraced the pink hue that can come with the interaction between the coconut water’s antioxidants and natural elements like light and temperature. Harmless Harvest’s commitment to sustainability and environmentally conscious practices extends beyond the bottle, too. The brand works with coconut growers in Thailand to source ethically farmed, non-GMO coconuts and also invests in initiatives that support farmers and their communities. item.title: SALES: Best AI Reputation Management Firms in 2026: Top Picks for AI Visibility & LLM Reputation (vs. Traditional ORM)
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
When someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity about your business, the answer they get is now your first impression. ChatGPT alone reached 900 million weekly active users in February 2026. Traditional online reputation management was built to push bad links off page one. AI visibility and LLM reputation management is about what the answer itself says. That shift has created a new category, and only a handful of companies work in it. Some are service firms that change what AI says. Others are software platforms that measure it. Below, we rank the best AI reputation management firms and platforms for 2026, explain how this work differs from traditional ORM, and show which option fits which need. What is AI visibility and LLM reputation management? AI visibility and LLM reputation management is the work of monitoring and shaping what large language models like ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews say about a person or brand. It covers two jobs: making sure accurate, positive information shows up in AI answers, and removing or correcting the false, outdated or harmful sources those answers are built on. How is it different from traditional ORM? Traditional online reputation management and AI reputation management share the same goal, but they work on different surfaces. ○ Traditional ORM: Ten blue links on Google, plus review sites. ○ AI reputation management: A single generated answer that blends many sources into one story. ○ Traditional ORM: A negative link is one result among many, and few people scroll past page one. ○ AI reputation management: A negative claim can become the whole answer. When Google shows an AI summary, users click a source inside it on just 1% of visits, according to Pew Research Center. ○ Traditional ORM: Suppression, publishing positive pages that outrank the bad one. ○ AI reputation management: Removing or correcting the source, because AI tools can still find and cite a page that’s been pushed to page three. ○ Traditional ORM: Keyword rankings. ○ AI reputation management: What each AI platform says, which sources it cites and how often your brand is recommended. We looked at four things: whether each company tracks what AI platforms say, whether it can change those answers, how many AI platforms it covers, and who it’s built for. Direct removal capability carried the most weight, since monitoring alone tells you about a problem without solving it. Several entries below are software platforms rather than service firms. We included them because many businesses will use a platform alongside a service firm, and knowing the difference helps you pick the right mix. The best AI reputation management firms and platforms in 2026 What they do: Reputation Resolutions is a full-service online reputation management firm based in Englewood, Colorado, and our pick for the top spot among the best AI reputation management firms. It is the only firm on this list that combines AI monitoring with hands-on removal of the content behind harmful answers. Its team audits what every major AI platform says about a client, traces each claim to the page it came from, removes or corrects that source, and builds accurate content to take its place. Standout capability: Removal at the source. Most companies on this list measure AI visibility. Reputation Resolutions changes it, with platform-specific work for ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. It has also built free tools that put that removal expertise in anyone’s hands: RemoveNews.ai writes a personalized removal request for a news article and finds the editor’s direct contact in about 60 seconds, and a free court record removal scan finds court and arrest records copied onto people-search and mugshot sites. Track record: More than a decade of removal work, more than 5,000 clients in over 40 countries, and recognition from Forbes and Inc. Magazine. Best for: Individuals, executives and businesses dealing with false, outdated or damaging AI answers, and anyone who needs the problem fixed rather than just reported. “We start every AI engagement the same way,” Will says. “We ask each platform what your customers would ask, record every source it cites, and then go after those sources one by one. That’s the only fix that holds across every AI tool at once.” What they do: Minc Law is a Cleveland-based law firm focused on internet defamation, online harassment and content removal. The firm says it has removed more than 200,000 pieces of defamatory and damaging online content and litigated more than 350 cases in 26 states and five countries. Standout capability: Legal action. When false content won’t come down through outreach or platform policies, Minc Law can send demand letters, pursue defamation claims and work to unmask anonymous posters. Best for: Cases where the source behind a harmful AI answer is defamatory and needs a legal remedy. It pairs well with a removal-focused reputation firm: legal pressure on one side, removal and AI reputation work on the other. What they do: Birdeye is a review and customer experience platform for multi-location brands. Its Birdeye AI Search product tracks brand and location-level visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Claude and Grok. Standout capability: Location-level AI visibility scoring, citation tracking and sentiment analysis, tied to its review management tools. Best for: Franchises and multi-location brands that want to monitor AI visibility location by location and keep review volume up. Keep in mind: Birdeye is software. It can show you a negative source and help you publish better content, but it doesn’t remove third-party articles, records or posts. What they do: Yext manages business listings and brand data across search engines, maps and directories. In March 2025 it launched Yext Scout, an AI search and competitive intelligence agent that tracks how brands appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok and Google. Standout capability: Keeping business facts accurate and consistent everywhere AI tools look, with competitor benchmarking built in. Best for: Enterprise and multi-location brands whose main AI problem is inconsistent or outdated business information. Keep in mind: Yext focuses on data you control, like listings and web content. It isn’t built to remove negative content published by others. What they do: Podium is a customer communication platform for local businesses that combines messaging, review requests and payments. Its AI Employee handles lead response and appointment booking around the clock. Standout capability: Generating a steady flow of fresh, positive reviews, which feed the review sites AI tools pull from when they describe local businesses. Best for: Local service businesses such as auto dealers, home services, dental and medical practices that want more reviews and faster customer response. Keep in mind: Podium builds positive signals. It doesn’t track AI answers directly or remove harmful content. What they do: Vendasta is a white-label software platform for agencies and resellers that serve small businesses. Its Reputation AI product monitors reviews across more than 100 sites and uses an AI agent to post personalized review replies. Standout capability: White-label delivery, so agencies can offer review and reputation tools under their own brand. Best for: Marketing agencies that want to add reputation services for many small business clients at once. Keep in mind: Vendasta is a toolset for agencies, not a removal service, and its focus is reviews rather than AI answers. What they do: Profound is an answer engine optimization (AEO) analytics platform that shows brands how often AI models mention them and in what context, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. The company raised $180 million at a $1.8 billion valuation in September 2026. Standout capability: Large-scale measurement of AI share of voice and citation patterns for enterprise marketing teams. Best for: Enterprise marketing and SEO teams that want detailed data on how their brand performs in AI answers compared with competitors. Keep in mind: Profound measures and optimizes visibility. It doesn’t handle reputation crises or remove harmful content. Which option is right for you? ● If AI is saying something false or damaging about you: Start with Reputation Resolutions. It’s the only option here that traces AI claims to their sources and removes them. ● If the source is defamatory and needs legal action: Add Minc Law. ● If you run many locations and want ongoing AI and review monitoring: Look at Birdeye or Yext. ● If you’re a local business that needs more reviews: Podium fits. ● If you’re an agency serving small businesses: Vendasta fits. ● If you’re an enterprise team measuring AI share of voice: Profound fits. AI visibility and LLM reputation management is quickly replacing page-one rankings as the measure of how people see you. Monitoring platforms can tell you what AI says, and review tools can build positive signals, but changing a harmful answer means removing what it’s built on. For anyone comparing the best companies for AI reputation management, that’s the deciding question: can they change the answer, or only report it? On that test, Reputation Resolutions ranks first.

item.title: SALES: 15 Best Grand Canyon Hotels, Rentals, and Glampsites for Sleeping in Style Under the Stars
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
A mile deep and 277 miles long, the Grand Canyon is a jaw-droppingly majestic chasm in Arizona’s rust-red desert that’s speckled with pinyon pines. Standing on its edge, one can’t help but feel small, watching the mighty Colorado River churn vigorously along the ravine’s bottom. Whether you’re hoping for a challenging all-day hike to the canyon’s floor, a soul-stirring overlook near the visitor center, or a multi-day rafting expedition, this national park has all that (and more) in spades. It’s hardly a surprise that it drew more than 4.4 million visitors in 2025 alone, so you know you'll have some competition when it comes to finding the best place to stay nearby. Personally, I like to stay as close as possible to the park, to make the most of dreamy desert sunrises and maximize my time on the trails. Grand Canyon is famous for its historic lodges and quirky Route 66 nostalgia, which can make picking the perfect spot for your crew a little overwhelming. Cozy cabin or fancy, family-sized rental? Canvas glamping tent under the stars or a fun getaway that’s in the heart of the action? I’ve sorted through the hundreds of options so you don’t have to. Here are my favorite Grand Canyon hotels, glamping sites, vacation rentals, and cabins for a memorable stay in and around this utterly striking national park. How to plan a trip to Grand Canyon National Park When is the best time to visit Grand Canyon National Park? With an elevation spanning 2,000 feet to 8,000 feet, Grand Canyon experiences a wide range of temperatures on any given day. Thus, the best season to visit greatly depends on what your adventure priorities are. If you’re planning to raft “the big ditch” with a guide, go between April and October for warm, sunny days that perfectly contrast the 50-degree Colorado River. Hoping to hike to the bottom and camp at Bright Angel? Don your favorite traction devices atop the canyon to crunch through seasonal ice and book a backcountry permit for late fall, winter, or early spring. Auto tourists who want to explore the canyon’s south rim by car can travel in virtually any season—just be prepared for crowds in summer months and occasional snow closures at the height of winter. Lastly, a good rule of thumb for intrepid travelers hiking down into the canyon is that you’ll gain roughly 5 degrees for every 1,000 feet you descend. Plan on it being 20 degrees warmer at the bottom of the canyon than it is at the rim. The National Park Service (NPS) does not recommend hiking to the bottom of the canyon during summer months, as temperatures at Phantom Ranch often surpass 100 degrees. How do you get to Grand Canyon National Park? If you’re planning to fly in, the closest major airports are Sky Harbor International in Phoenix and Harry Reid International in Las Vegas, but both are at least a three-hour drive away, so you’ll want to rent a car and crank up the tunes to brave the journey. Regional airports are scattered around the area, most notably in small-but-commercial Flagstaff, Sedona, and Tusayan. There’s also a vintage train service that runs daily from Williams, Arizona. Notably, Grand Canyon National Park is a stone’s throw away from one of the most iconic road trips the US has to offer–historic Route 66. Running from Chicago all the way to the Pacific Coast in Santa Monica, California, this legendary trip ventures across northern Arizona on Interstate 40. What are the best things to do in Grand Canyon National Park? Spanning 23 breathtaking miles between Grand Canyon Village and the Desert View area, Desert View Drive is the only scenic byway in the park that’s open year-round to private vehicles. Enjoy Mary Colter’s iconic Desert View Watchtower, which was inspired by ancestral Puebloan architecture and features murals by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie, at the park’s far eastern edge. Another popular drive along the South Rim is the winding Hermit Road, which ends at the historic stone structure of Hermit’s Rest that date back to 1914. The drive is only open to private vehicles in December, January, and February; in all other months, travelers must use the park’s free shuttle system, hopping on and off at popular sites. Though the hiking distance between the canyon’s north and south rims is a scant 21 miles, the drive to get between the two is a circuitous 220 miles. As a result, only 10% of the national park’s visitors set foot on the just-as-striking North Rim. This high-elevation outpost (over 8,000 feet) and log cabin-style lodge have a shorter visitation season than the South Rim (you’ll have to travel there between May 15 and October 15 most years), but adventurous drivers desperate to escape the crowds should make a beeline for the pinyon and ponderosa pine–studded views of crumbling crimson sandstone along Cape Royal Road. Plus, you’ll be within easy driving distance of Zion, if you’d like to extend your journey. If you’re into hiking past dramatic vermillion outcroppings, secret waterfalls, and hanging gardens, you’re in the right place. The Grand Canyon also boasts some of the most stunning wheelchair-accessible paths in the country (check out the 13-mile, mostly-paved Rim Trail), as well as hamstring-busting overnight treks into the belly of the ravine. For an epic out-and-back excursion with much of the expansive red rock scenery you’d find on a longer jaunt, head to South Kaibab Trailhead and venture just under a mile downhill to the aptly named Ooh Aah Point. Want a little more bang for your buck? Continue down to Skeleton Point for a sweeping panorama of the Colorado River (six miles round trip). Bright Angel Trailhead is another iconic starting point for a day hike or overnight trek into the canyon. Lace up your boots for a three-mile round-trip stroll to the shade structure at Mile-and-a-Half Resthouse or, if you’re an experienced hiker looking to sweat, start early for an all-day 12-mile journey to jaw-dropping views of Plateau Point. Trekking to the bottom of the Grand Canyon and back is the stuff hiking bucket lists are made of. But due to midday heat and the extremely strenuous nature of these hikes, the National Park Service does not recommend aiming to complete such a journey in a single day. It’s highly recommended to nab a backcountry permit and camp overnight at one of the many below-the-rim sites (like Bright Angel Campground or Havasupai Gardens). Pro tip: Use the free park shuttle and create a loop starting at South Kaibab and ending at the Bright Angel Trailhead. Heading for the quieter North Rim? Tramp down the North Kaibab Trail for two miles (one-way) to Supai Tunnel. It’s rare that a national park offers a designated bike path along its most iconic sights, but at the Grand Canyon, visitors can spin for roughly 13 miles along the park’s dreamy South Rim vistas. BYO-bike or rent one at Canyon Adventures in the village, then steer onto the paved Greenway Trail to South Kaibab. Or, utilize the free shuttle system (yes, they’ve got bike racks) and ride the bus to Monument Creek Vista, then cruise along the South Rim to Hermits Rest. North Rim visitors hoping to escape that South Rim fervor can enjoy loads of rugged mountain biking. A 12-mile swath of the enormous, 800-mile Arizona Trail runs right through the park. Are there guided tours at Grand Canyon National Park? There are dozens of phenomenal guided tours available for guests who aren’t comfortable backpacking alone or want a unique type of experience. Mule rides are a storied part of the canyon’s past and how many early tourists ventured into the canyon (sometimes in full Victorian regalia). Though it might seem like a rough place for a working animal, mules are much better equipped to handle heat and steep, rocky terrain than their horse counterparts. Plus, these rides offer below-the-rim access for visitors with mobility concerns. Today, both short day trips and extended overnight ventures to Phantom Ranch on muleback are available for those looking to pay homage to a bygone era. For a brag-worthy addition to your hiking checklist, seek out Wildland Trekking’s guided rim-to-rim backpacking journeys (or, in winter, go big and test your skills on a rim-to-rim-to-rim hike). Craving something off the beaten path? The remote, five-day Hermit Loop offers miles of fire-red sandstone plateaus. I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the second-to-none river rafting to be had at Grand Canyon National Park. Grand Canyon Expeditions and Western River Expeditions have been guiding for decades and both offer first-class service for intrepid travelers looking to go the distance on the mighty Colorado. If your new external SSD doesn’t perform up to snuff, talk to the vendor about a firmware update, or use a Thunderbolt cable of suitable speed, which is how we solved the issue for testing. Thunderbolt cables are generally of far higher quality than some commodity USB cables. Why you should trust PCWorld for external drive reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld’s reviewers have been testing PC hardware for decades. Our storage evaluations are thorough and rigorous, pushing the limits of every product — from performance benchmarks to the practicalities of daily use. As PC users ourselves, we know what makes a product stand out. Only the best external drives make this list. Corsair EX300U – Best 10Gbps external SSD - Magnetic attachement to metal surfaces - Almost as pricey as 20Gbps SSDs currently Who should buy the Corsair EX300U? In normal times, this is the recommended option for anyone looking for an affordable that’s still “fast enough” — or anyone who is currently saddled with a USB 3.2 port that’s limited to 10Gbps speed. But these are not normal times, so our advice is to check current prices before buying. For instance, you can find this fantastic little magnetic square of a drive for 1TB / $117 on Amazon as of this writing. That’s about $17 more than it cost when I reviewed the drive, making it a still-reasonable price in this time of extreme NAND-price inflation. But if you want to step up to 2TB, Amazon is asking a jaw-dropping and $290. That’s more than the 2TB version of our favorite 20Gbps drive below. Price disparities aside, the EX300U is the fastest 10Gbps SSD I’ve tested to date, besting the Teamgroup X2 Max listed below by a small margin. And unlike the latter, you can stick it to a metal object like a PC case via the circular magnet on the back. Note that aluminum is not particularly magnetic, so this doesn’t work with most Macs. The warranty on the EX300U is three years, which is the usual for external SSDs, but the 250TBW (terabytes that can be written) per terabyte of capacity is a little stingy. At least Corsair provides a TBW rating — most vendors don’t for external SSDs. Still, the odds of anyone exceeding that TBW limit is rather low. Most of the time games are reading data, not writing it. Teamgroup X2 Max – Best USB stick / thumb drive - Excellent 10Gbps performer, even with long writes Who should buy the Teamgroup X2 Max? Anyone seeking top-performance in the classic fits-easily-in-a-shirt-pocket thumb drive form-factor should be looking to the Teamgroup X2 Max. It’s small even for a thumb drive, and just as fast as almost any 10Gbps SSD — small or large — that we’ve tested. The X2 Max uses NVMe storage internally which accounts for the performance. Externally, it conveniently provides both captive Type-C and Type-A connectors so you don’t have to drag around cables or adapters. Teamgroup X2 Max: Further considerations It’s relatively pricey compared to a commodity thumb drive, but the performance is well worth it. Put bluntly — there’s no better option if fast thumb drive storage is what you seek. - Handsome, IP65-rated design (dust-proof, water-resistant) Who should buy the PNY RP60? If your laptop supports USB 3.2×2 for 20Gbps performance and you want to take full advantage of it, and/or you’re not the most careful person with hardware, this ruggedized external SSD is a practical way to ward off accidental damage. The PNY RP60 offers more than just a rugged IP65-rated exterior that protects against dust and water droplets. It’s handsome and lightweight to boot, as well as an admirable performer, even besting one of the fastest 20Gbps drives I’ve tested — the Crucial X10 Pro — in a couple of our tests. A 20Gbps SSD is the sweet spot in the price/performance ratio for external SSDs. The only issue is that the USB 3.2×2 drives function at only 10Gbps or slower unless attached to a dedicated 20Gbps port. That applies to most USB4 and Thunderbolt ports as well. The RP60 is competitively priced at $180 and $230 for 1TB and 2TB, respectively. Note that these prices are significantly higher than when I first reviewed the RP60 due to the global NAND shortage. Addlink P30 – Best budget USB4 external SSD - Over 3GBps reading and 2.5GBps writing - Slightly off the performance pace for USB4 Who should buy the Addlink P30? Those looking for USB4 performance without breaking the bank should be shopping Addlink’s P30. It’s priced more like a 10Gbps SSD than a 40Gbps model, and while it’s the slowest USB4 drive we’ve tested, that’s like saying it’s the slowest F1 car on the grid — it’s still plenty fast. Additionally, the P30 is super handy for anyone looking to add semi-permanent external storage to a PC with a metal case — there’s a magnetic ring that allows you to “stick” the drive in place. Add in a small form-factor and good looks and you have yourself a winner. Using modern TLC, the P30’s write rate only drops to around 800Mbps when it runs out of secondary cache. That makes it a workable drive even for pros. It’s also one of the few drives that is likely a better bargain than rolling your own with an external enclosure such as TerraMaster’s D1 SSD Plus. Samsung P9 – Best 40Gbps USB4 external SSD - Fast and sustains long writes exceptionally well - Runs remarkably cool despite its diminutive dimensions - Like all current SSDs — very expensive Who should buy the Samsung P9? Anyone who wants stellar sustained throughput, but for less cash than an 80Gbps SSD (if you can even find one of those these days!), should look to the Samsung P9. Note that a 40Gbps USB4 external SSD isn’t for everyone. Your PC needs to support the USB4 or the Thunderbolt 3/4/5 spec in order to take advantage of its capabilities — and while cheaper than 80Gbps, it’s still not cheap by any stretch. If you’re equipped to enter the club, the Samsung P9 will reward you with nearly 4GBps transfers at a more affordable price than our previous pick for USB4, the Adata SE920 — which has catapulted to $556 for 1TB, compared to the P9’s MSRP of $340. Of course, with all storage right now, availability is another story. Still you can find the 2TB P9 on Amazon for $650. Besides being very fast, the P9 is (theoretically) a good pick for anyone who wants performance and capacity, with sizes up to 8TB — again, availability being the deciding factor. There are a few other things that distinguish the P9: It’s extremely svelte, and thus extra portable; it’s able to maintain speed even when running very large data sets, while also remaining cool; and it comes with a nice 5-year warranty. SanDisk Desk Drive 10Gbps – Best external SSD for backups - Available in large 4TB and 8TB capacities - Attractive and unusual, if somewhat large, heat-shedding design Who should buy the SanDisk Desk Drive? Anyone who needs lots of room for data plus the speed of an SSD should be shopping for the SanDisk Desk Drive, which is available with up to 8TB of capacity. As the name suggests, the SanDisk Desk Drive isn’t nearly as portable as the other drives in this list. Partly because it’s a bit too bulky for a pocket or laptop bag, but primarily because it requires an AC adapter. It’s hardly a behemoth; it’s just not as convenient as a pure bus-powered unit for transport. The Desk Drive is aimed at users with more sedentary work scenarios, to function as auxiliary storage and a fast backup medium. That’s also evident in the fact that it ships only in 4GB and 8GB capacities. SanDisk Desk Drive: Further considerations Granted, the Desk Drive costs a lot more per-gigabyte than you’d pay for a backup hard drive. But that surcharge buys you brisk 10Gbps performance, and the assurance that comes from an SSD’s lack of moving parts, i.e. susceptibility to wear and shock damage. In other words, its speed, ruggedness, and reliability make it worth more than an HDD. WD My Passport, Works with USB C – Best portable hard drive Who should buy the WD Passport, Works with USB-C? Those looking for capacity without the high price should be looking at 2.5-inch external hard drives, and this capacious drive in particular. We can forgive the cumbersome name, and the fact that this drive, misleadingly, doesn’t actually feature a Type-C port (but rather an adapter), because there is a misconception among some that Type-C will make a portable hard drive faster. It won’t. In the end this drive has the best combination of price, capacity, and performance in its class. For starters, the WD My Passport, Works with USB-C offers a ton of capacity — up to 6TB — and at a far more affordable price per terabyte than one can get from an SSD (a little less than $30/TB versus $60 to $80 for the latter). This makes the WD My Passport a natural fit for backup, particularly during off hours when an SSD’s superior speed won’t really save you any time. WD Passport, Works with USB-C: Further considerations As for the misleading moniker, the My Passport does indeed work with USB-C, but it’s by way of the drive’s bundled Micro-B to Type-A cable and Type-A to USB-C adapter. Yup, the port is the much older Micro-B. Mind you, WD’s My Passport Ultra drives, which actually do feature a USB-C port, don’t perform any faster than this drive, and cost a bit more. In fact, the My Passport performs on par with the best of 2.5-inch hard drives we’ve tested, while being the best deal. If it’s a portable, high-capacity hard drive that you’re after — pick this one. Seagate Expansion Desktop – Best desktop hard drive - Twice the sustained throughput of 2.5-inch external HDDs Who should buy the Seagate Expansion Desktop? Users looking for the most capacity for the least amount of cash, should definitely be checking out the 3.5-inch Seagate Expansion Desktop. It’s available with up to 28TB of capacity — more than three times the current maximum for SSDs The Desktop Expansion also delivers twice the sustained transfer rate of the average 2.5-inch external hard drives — our 16TB test unit read and wrote at close to 280MBps. Nice. As mentioned, all this storage comes at a very competitive price point, hovering around $30 per terabyte, compared to the $70 per terabyte an external SSD costs. Seagate Expansion Desktop: Further considerations The relevant caveat with all HDDs is that they are more likely to fail than SSDs, and important data on them should be backed up regularly. Alternatively, you can run them in mirrored (RAID 1) pairs, though that cuts into the bargain price per terabyte by quite a bit. As we said in our review of the drive: “If you deal with large amounts of data, you can’t beat a high-capacity hard drive for gathering it into one place.” This is the drive we’d pick for that job. - Kingston Dual Portable flash drive: Competitive on 10Gbps performance, but not on price. - SanDisk Extreme Pro Dual: A versatile 10Gbps with both Type-A and Type-C connectors. - SanDisk Crayola flash drive: Not the fastest drive, but it’s serviceable and cute as heck. - Adata SC735: A super-compact thumb drive SSD best for light-duty chores. - PNY Duo Link V3: A good-performing 10Gbps thumb drive with both Type-C/Type-A connectors. - Satechi DotDisk SSD enclosure: For DIYers, this is by far the most portable 80Gbps enclosure we’ve reviewed thanks to fan cooling. - Adata SD820: Delivers excellent 20Gbps performance in a small and rugged package. - Teamgroup PD20: Another SSD that’s best for light duty, albeit with an elegant and tough exterior. - Teamgroup T-Create P31: A convenient, secure SSD for videographers and content creators. - TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus: An enclosure that let’s you build your own 40Gbps SSD. - Asus TUF Gaming A2: Offers a rugged DIY external SSD option for USB3.2×2. - Seagate One Touch USB hard drive: Using a 3.5 hard drive, and models expected to reach up to 24TB, this is one of the cheapest ways to add terabytes to your system. Drive tests currently utilize Windows 11 24H2, 64-bit running off of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro in an Asus Z890-Creator WiFi (PCIe 4.0/5.0) motherboard. The CPU is a Core Ultra i5 225 feeding/fed by two Kingston Fury 32GB DDR5 4,800MHz modules (64GB of memory total). Both 20Gbps USB and Thunderbolt 5 are integrated and Intel CPU/GPU graphics are used. SSDs involved in the test are mounted in either a HighPoint 7604A 16x 4-slot PCIe 5.0 RAID adapter card or a single-slot Asus ROG M.2 PCIe 5.0 adapter. We run the CrystalDiskMark 8, AS SSD 2, and ATTO 4 synthetic benchmarks to find the storage device’s potential performance, then a series of 48GB and 450GB transfers tests using Windows Explorer drag-and-drop to show what you’ll see under Window, as well as the far faster FastCopy to show what’s possible. A two-drive 25GBps RAID 0 array on the HighPoint 7604A 16x PCIe 5.0 adapter card is used as the secondary source/destination. Each test is performed on an NTFS-formatted and newly TRIM’d drive so the results are optimal. Note that in normal use, as a drive fills up, performance may decrease due to less NAND for secondary caching, as well as other factors. This can be less of a factor with the current crop of SSDs with far faster late-generation NAND. Caveat: The performance numbers shown apply only to the drive we were shipped and to the capacity tested. SSD performance can and will vary by capacity due to more or fewer chips to shotgun reads/writes across and the amount of NAND available for secondary caching. Vendors also occasionally swap components. If you ever notice a large discrepancy between the performance you experience and that which we report, by all means, let us know. Note also that some of the SSDs in this roundup were tested using other equipment and methodologies which you can read about in the standalone reviews. To learn more about our testing methodology see PCWorld’s article on how we test external SSDs. Who curated this article? Jon L Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. There are four general categories when it comes to external storage, all fairly self-explanatory: portable SSD, portable HDD, desktop HDD (typically larger capacity, larger footprint, and requiring external power, and thus meant to be stationary), and thumb-drive SSD — the smallest and most portable external storage, but often limited in capacity. If you’re looking to treat your external storage as an extension of your internal storage, then performance is likely paramount. You’ll want an SSD, which can be 10 to 20 times faster — depending on the interface — than a hard drive. SSDs also offer sub-millisecond seek times where HDDs seek at tens of milliseconds. On the other hand, if the primary role is backup, then you might want to opt for a hard drive (HDD) with its larger capacity and a significantly lower price per gigabyte/terabyte. Currently, single SSDs top out at 8TB, 2.5-inch HDDs at 6TB, and desktop 3.5-inch HDDs at 36TB. Need internal storage instead? See our guides to the best SSDs and best PCIe 4.0 SSDs. The cost per TB of both SSDs and HDDs tends to drop as capacity increases. However, the latest, greatest (highest capacity) drives of both types tend to carry a premium, simply because the company knows some users want as much capacity as they can get and are willing to pay more. Normally, you’ll get the lowest price per terabyte from the second-highest capacity drive, aka last years model. But do the math before you plunk down your hard earned money — you may find deals. Below you can see the phenomenon in terms of a WD 2.5-inch HDD. Above you can see the general more capacity, cheaper per terabyte trend. How much external storage capacity do you need? If you’re extending your internal storage, you probably know better than we do how much you’ll need. Video sucks up space at a remarkable pace, especially at higher resolutions. With SSDs, traditionally we’ve recommended twice the capacity you think you’ll need as older types tended to slow down as they filled. Modern SSD controller design has mitigated this to a great degree, but it’s still our rule of thumb. If you’re going for backup, then the more the merrier. Again, twice the amount of total data on the drives to back up is a good start. Remember, you’ll want at least one full system backup, then regular incremental, differential, or data-only backups. That said, reinstalling Windows and your applications isn’t quite the insane drudgery it once was, and you can likely get away with just backing up your data. In that case twice the amount of essential data you have will do the trick. Sensing a 2X trend here? Another rule of thumb: 1TB for travel and light backups, 2TB for mainstream photo/video libraries, 4TB+ for larger archives, 8TB+ for desk-bound bulk backup. Note that these are our minimum recommendations. The more the merrier, and the further back in time you can keep backups for. Which external interface should you opt for? If you’re buying an HDD, the interface is relatively unimportant — even older 5Gbps USB offers more than enough bandwidth to accommodate the 300MBps that is as fast as a modern HDD can deliver data. In fact, you’re unlikely to run across an external HDD that offers a faster interface unless it’s a multi-bay RAID box. Even then, 10Gbps is likely to be more than fast enough. For SSDs, there’s a huge difference in performance depending on the interface involved. The internals of most external SSDs these days are NVMe rather than SATA, and capable of 3GBps. No matter what the internals, 5Gbps USB (3.0) limits the drive to just over 500MBps, 10Gbps USB (3.2) to just over 1GBps, and 20Gbps USB (3.2×2)/Thunderbolt 2 to around 2GBps, so you’re leaving performance on the table with any of those. Of course, those may be all that your computer offers, so buy to match. However, if you’re rocking a newer computer you may have Thunderbolt 3/4/5 or if it’s really recent, USB4. Those will deliver around 3.5GBps unless they’re the still rare 80Gbps flavors in which case you’ll see around 6.5GBps. Note that all those numbers are what you’ll see with synthetic benchmarks. Windows Explorer is a horrible performer in data transfers. We recommend using FastCopy or if you’re a command line type — Xcopy. Both of which are two to three times as fast as Explorer transferring large files. Compatibility is a major concern and where 5Gbps and 10Gbps USB reign supreme. You’d be hard pressed to find a computer or device that won’t support them and they function on nearly every USB and Thunderbolt port in existence. USB 3.2×2 on the other hand requires a dedicated 20Gbps port or a newer USB4 port to function at the full 20Gbps speed. They drop to 10Gbps on 10Gbps USB ports and most Thunderbolt ports. Obviously, 40Gbps USB4 requires a USB4 port or Thunderbolt 4/5 port to reach maximum speed. But on USB4 ports, even that’s not guaranteed. We haven’t seen one yet, but full 40Gbps implementation in true USB Forum fashion, isn’t required, so there might be slower 20Gbps USB4 SSDs and ports. Thunderbolt SSDs generally require a Thunderbolt 3/4/5 port or USB4 port to function at 40Gbps. In truth, USB4 is basically Thunderbolt 4 with some minor tweaks. 80Gbps Thunderbolt SSDs require a Thunderbolt 5 port, and/or the upcoming 80Gbps USB4 second gen. USB4 SSDs are easily the most compatible (backwards to USB 2.x, forward to Thunderbolt 5) high-performance types, so they’re currently our recommended interface for speedy data delivery. That said, 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 is pretty sexy. What connector type should you use? Though the industry is generally on board with Type-C connectors at this point, you may still find some older types around. From top to bottom in the image below: Mini-USB, Micro B SuperSpeed, SuperSpeed Micro B, Thunderbolt 2/mini DisplayPort, and Type-C. You’ll also find the occasional Lightning connector drive (not shown). More complete descriptions follow below. While we of course recommend orientation-agnostic Type-C, you can find Type-C adapters or adapter cables for any type. USB Type-C, USB-C, Type-C is the latest USB connector and the one the world is standardizing on. It’s small, easy to insert, and you don’t have to worry about which side faces up as with Type-A. Keep in mind that Type-C refers only to the connector itself. What is carried over the wires varies greatly: USB 2.0 High Speed (480Mbps) to USB 3.2 SuperSpeed 20Gbps, as well as USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4/5 and any combination of them. USB Type-A: You won’t find this familiar rectangular port on any drive, but you will still find it on plenty of PCs and laptops as well as the male version on the other end of most Type-B and Type-C adapter cables. USB 3 Micro-B is the wider, flatter port that’s still very common on many lower-cost portable and desktop external hard drives. It’s actually the same Micro USB port used on older phones, but with more data lines to hit USB 3.0 speeds. It’ll do 5Gbps and is fine for hard drives and SATA (internally) SSDs. Micro-B cables are generally Type-A on the PC end. USB 3 Type-B is the larger, squarer version of USB 3.0 Micro B. Type B ports are becoming rare, though you might find one on older 5.25-inch enclosures, printers, and scanners. It supports speeds up to 5Gbps and cables are generally Type-A on the PC side. Thunderbolt 2 is dead at this point. It’s found on older Macs, but even Apple put it out to pasture in 2017. There’s no need to invest in a Thunderbolt 2 drive unless it’s for legacy support issues. That said… …Apple sells a bi-directional Thunderbolt 1/2 to 3 adapter if you need to connect the one generation to the other. The adapter does not, however, carry power, so bus-powered external drives (no power jack) will require a powered dock. eSATA is another legacy port that’s disappeared from newer devices. Created for attaching external storage to your computer’s SATA bus, eSATA was a cheap way in its day to move beyond the toddling 60MBps performance of USB 2.0. 5Gbps USB 3.0 put the last nail in eSATA’s coffin. As with Thunderbolt 2, the only reason to invest in an eSATA drive is for use with older computers. Multiple drives for backup? We discussed the rule of three for backup, but while the cloud is a great offsite option, you can also manage that with multiple external drives — storing them in different locations. Once upon a time, I used to regularly send copies of my recordings to my mom’s for safe-keeping. If you’re using your external storage as a primary repository for important data, then you should have a second drive as a copy. You might even consider a dual-drive enclosure and run them mirrored, i.e. the same set of data written simultaneously to both. SSDs aren’t nearly as prone to mishap as hard drives, but even then… Simply put, keep your data backed up! For more guidance on building out the best backup plan possible, see our roundups of the best cloud backup services and best Windows backup software. What’s the best external SSD? Consumers have a lot of excellent external SSDs to choose from. If speed is important, the best 40Gbps external drive is the Adata SE920 at 40Gbps; for 20Gbps performance, and a significant cost savings, consider the PNY RP60; for the best balance of performance and price, we recommend the 10Gbps Corsair EX300U. What’s the best USB thumb drive? Currently, the Teamgroup X2 Max is the pick of the litter. It’s super slim, but capacious, cheetah fast, and has both Type-C and Type-A connectors. What’s the best external hard drive? If you’re looking for portability, get WD’s My Passport, Works with USB-C (note that it uses an adapter for USB-C, not a native USB-C port). If you’re looking for capacity, then it’s Seagate’s Expansion Desktop. What is the difference between an SSD and an HDD? HDDs (hard disk drives) are essentially boxes containing spinning platters with read/write arms that skim across them to detect the orientation of, or re-align particles in the magnetic material that coats the platters. SSDs (solid state drives), on the other hand, use flash memory and have no moving parts inside the drive. Data is instead stored in cells — aka, voltage traps — which are interconnected in a matrix. The matrix approach allows for data to be pushed or pulled to/from many different places at once and significantly increases both read and write speed — on the order of 100 times faster currently. Generally speaking, SSDs are a better bet for your external drives due to their smaller size, faster speeds, and far superior durability. The main drawback to SSDs is that you pay quite a bit more per terabyte of storage. As technology and production techniques improve, the price of SSDs has and will continue to drop. How often should you back up your data? As often as possible, i.e. at roughly the rate that it changes. This is especially true if you are working on an important project or have data that you absolutely cannot afford to lose. The key point here is that if your drive goes belly up, everything added since your last backup is toast. If you have your external drive connected to your computer at all times, it is a good idea to automate the backup process and have the drive back up your data as it changes, or every hour or so. Otherwise, connect and back up at least once a day. See our roundups of the best Windows backup software and the best online backup services to learn more. Even if you work with your data in the cloud, a local backup is a very good idea. We know of no major service that’s lost data, but there’s always a first time. Why does Windows say my external drive is smaller than specified? This is because of the difference between the binary and decimal number systems, their nomenclatures, and a Microsoft miscue. Your 2TB drive indeed has two trillion bytes of storage, and if you look at the byte count that Windows displays in a drive’s properties dialog, this should be what you see. This, in the International System of Units (SI/decimal), is two terabytes, or 2TB. This is the standard language vendors use as consumers are far more familiar with base 10. However, Windows uses the newer International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) binary multiples 2^10 (Kibibyte/KiB), 2^20 (Mebibyte/MiB), 2^30 (Gibibyte/Gib). Binary multiples are larger numbers (one KiB is 1,024) so when Windows divides the total bytes by the IEC system, the you get something like 1.8TiB for a 2TB drive. Alas, Windows labels this as 1.8TB, misleading the user. Other reasons you might not see as much available storage in the properties tab are formatting or partitioning. The file system uses some storage for file location and size info, etc. Also, some drives come with a small partition containing software so the main partition will be smaller than the drive’s total capacity. How long will my external drive last? The lifespan of an external hard drive can be anywhere from three minutes to 10 years or more depending on make and model, as well as the amount of use and operating environment. They’re mechanical devices subject to wear and susceptible to shock damage, so they should be kept cool and treated gently. Reliability has increased dramatically over the last decade. Alas, judging the likely lifespan of an external hard drive is a crap shoot. Of course check the warranty, but the MTBF (Mean Time Before Failure) number is generally considered fantasy within the industry. Peruse user feedback which can provide insight into long term usage, and keep your ears peeled for strange noises, your fingers crossed, and don’t drop the thing! Our best guess is that you should get at least five years with careful handling. SSDs don’t wear out or break mechanically, but their cells can only be written to so many times. SSDs generally have a TBW (terabytes that may be written) rating, but this is rarely provided by vendors for external SSDs. Hint: They may not use the same SSD inside throughout the product lifespan. Most internal M.2 NVMe TLC SSDs are rated for around 600TBW per terabyte, and QLC types for around 200TBW, though the type of NAND in use is also rarely provided by vendors. That’s a lot of data, and a lot of SSDs are rated well below what they might achieve. You can guesstimate by using a utility to see how much data you write to an SSD a day and then doing the math. External SSD warranties are generally between three and five years, but as with all such things, it’s a financial risk calculation for the company. As is the TBW. Our best guess based on experience is perhaps a decade. However, certain models have had issues long before that — generally due to a flaw or failure in the bridge chip or controller. How do external drives fail? There are a few of ways that an external hard drive might fail. The motor might quit, the read/write heads might crash into the platter surface due to shock while operating, or the electronics might overheat and go belly up. You might get a warning in the form of strange noises such as a scraping or grinding sound. If the data is particularly important, turn it off immediately and call a recovery service. That scraping sound may be the coating on the platter being removed by a crashed head. This is unrecoverable. If you keep running it, back it up immediately and replace it. SSDs generally go belly up due to the increasingly rare controller failure, which is a relatively easy fix/reset for someone who knows the SSD’s internals such as a recovery service. SSDs will also eventually wear out, though this only precludes further writing to the unit. You can still read what’s on the drive, so it’s not the disaster a HDD failure can be. What’s the fastest external interface? In order, the fastest PC external interfaces are currently: 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5, 40Gbps USB4/Thunderbolt 3 and 4, 20Gbps USB 3.2×2, 10GBps USB 3.2, then 5Gbps USB 3.x. What’s the most compatible external interface? In order of compatibility: USB4, Thunderbolt 3/4/5, USB 3.x, USB 3.2×2, USB 3.x, USB 2, and USB 1.1.

Liverpool enjoys a well-deserved reputation for its cultural prowess, but there’s more to this city than the Beatles museum and football. Travellers have made full use of Liverpool’s hotel scene in recent years after the city played host to Eurovision in 2023 and Taylor Swift in 2024, but visitors shouldn't forget about Airbnb. There are a slew of wonderful homestays to book in this northern cultural hub, offering an authentic slice of Liverpudlian life, often at a much cheaper price than a typical night in a hotel.
