item.title: SALES: 14 Best Steakhouses in New York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
No single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak. Read our complete New York City guide here, which includes: - Read Full ReviewSeagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel important. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H. - Read Full Review372 Fulton Street, Downtown Brooklyn Gage & Tollner is more than 100 years old, but somehow manages to feel exactly like a Brooklyn restaurant of today should: inviting, thoughtful, and bustling—with a dose of history mixed in for good measure. It’s the type of restaurant that reminds guests why New York is a great city to dine in. The landmarked interior at Gage & Tollner is lined with mirrors and cherry wood arches and lit by brass chandeliers. It’s precisely the type of place to order a classic cocktail, like one of the seven martinis on offer or a Manhattan. The menu leans into steakhouse classics like New York strip steak and shrimp cocktail, but there are more modern touches here too like clams kimsino, made with bacon-kimchi butter, and crispy hen of the woods mushrooms with black garlic aioli and house Sriracha. No matter your dinner order, make sure you save room for the baked Alaska created by former pastry chef Caroline Schiff, who was named a Best New Chef by Food & Wine in 2022. Under a large singed meringue coat sits layers of fresh mint, dark chocolate, and amarena cherry ice cream and chocolate cookie crunch. —Devra Ferst, contributor - Read Full Review4 Charles St, West Village, Manhattan The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a new friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate. 4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded. And so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor - Read Full Review178 Broadway, Williamsburg, Brooklyn Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the New York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H. - Read Full Review224 Lafayette St, SoHo, Manhattan This summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one. - Read Full Review16 West 22 St, Flatiron, Manhattan Head 10 blocks south of New York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F. - Read Full Review228 W 52nd Street, Midtown Manhattan Gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H. - Read Full Review72 W 36th Street, Midtown Manhattan The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the New-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren - Read Full Review1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan From the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—big leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa. Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell - Read Full Review355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel - Read Full Review513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan Buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S. - Read Full Review1 Fifth Avenue, West Village, Manhattan Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's New York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H. - Read Full Review56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is currently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, said to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs - Read Full Review305 W 48th St, Midtown Manhattan Dinner and a show in New York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu

item.title: SALES: 18 best bars in Soho our London editors are currently drinking at
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Soho has been at the epicentre of London's entertainment and nightlife scene for centuries – so it's no surprise that these days, the best bars in Soho are among some of the finest drinking dens in London. Originally established as a district for the aristocracy, by the 19th century, this corner of the West End was known for its theatres, public houses and sex workers. Fast forward 200 years – these days, Soho is a popular neighbourhood with remnants of that edgy spirit (although it's largely been cleaned up). Here, you're as likely to find buzzy pubs where smokers spill onto the streets for post-work pints as cosy wine bars or cutting-edge cocktail menus for date nights. Some of the best bars here are attached to the best restaurants in Soho – making them great for pre- or post-supper drinks. Others are indie drinking spots where you can find award-winning concoctions. Many are set on Soho's best-known streets – strolling Greek Street or Old Compton Street with a keen eye will reveal great little places to dive into. These are our favourites among all the bars in Soho. When choosing new bars, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out drinks, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly.

item.title: SALES: Where is it hot in February? Our top 15 destinations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
“Where is it hot in February?” is a question we travel editors always get asked during winter. And we get it – it’s always good to have something to look forward to during the colder, darker months. What better time of year to have a getaway booked in the diary than February, coming as it does after the comedown from the festive period? It’s when long-haul favourites come into their own, with some of the best destinations in February for winter sun including the likes of Jamaica, Thailand and Bali, where temperatures promise to be hot, hot, hot. Of course, those who don’t fancy jet lag can always turn to the warmest climes in Europe: think Malta, Sicily and of course, the Canary Islands, which can guarantee temperatures in the high teens or early 20s if you’re lucky. Looking for something closer to home? Our editors have also gathered their favourite European destinations to catch some sun in February. Where is it hot in February and cheap? If budget is an issue for you, but you still want to catch some rays, then stick to Europe: the Canary Islands in particular have a lot to offer in terms of value for money as well as scorching temperatures. Similarly, while the flight to Thailand may be pricey, once you get there, it’s possible to stay in relative luxury for far less than you would pay closer to home. Which countries are hot in February? As a rule of thumb, those closer to the Equator are warm year-round: think the Caribbean, Singapore and Kenya, for example. And for countries in the Southern Hemisphere, February is still their summer season, so the likes of South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand are all especially hot at this time of year too. Where is the best tropical vacation in February? The best tropical vacation in February for you will depend on how far you want to travel, and whether or not warm weather mixed with tropical storms is an issue for you. A safe bet is usually Thailand, as it’s the dry season at this time of year.

item.title: SALES: 3 more Ryobi tools you should buy before winter
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Winter is coming, and that means it's time to start preparing. Gear up for storms, gather some firewood, and get those winter tools ready. And if you don't have any winter tools, you'll be glad to hear that Ryobi has all sorts of practical tools you'll love when the temperatures plummet. As every DIYer knows, Ryobi makes a little bit of everything, from drills and drivers to strong impact wrenches, fans, leaf blowers, saws, and so much more. But for whatever reason, many people don't know that your favorite green tool brand also makes battery-powered snow shovels, heaters, and even snowblowers. We highlighted several great Ryobi winter tools last month, and here are a few more products you'll love. Staying warm is pretty important, especially when the mercury drops. Whether you're working in the garage, camping, hunting, tailgating, or dealing with an emergency power outage, you'll want Ryobi's brand-new 18V Portable Propane Heater. Portable models like the Buddy Heater are great, but Ryobi has a new model arriving at Home Depot this month that's just in time for winter. This isn't your average portable propane heater. For starters, it can deliver up to 13,000 BTU of heat output, has multiple heat modes, and includes a built-in fan for warmth coverage of around 325 sq. ft. It works like a regular heater without the battery: add your propane, press and hold to light, and enjoy warm hands and a toasty garage. But then, there's a Ryobi HEATBOOST technology mode that'll use your 18V battery to push all that hot air directly where you want it. Yes, there's a built-in fan you can use to direct the heat to a specific area, and it'll heat an entire room more easily with increased air movement. Best of all, that 18V battery will last longer than your propane tank, so make sure you bring a few extras. It's worth mentioning that there's a built-in door that completely seals off and protects your tank and battery from the elements, as well as an easy-carry handle for portability. With 13,000 BTU and hours of runtime, this portable propane heater from Ryobi will be your best friend this winter. A common occurrence during the cold winter months is a dead car battery. No one wants to be late for work, or even worse, stranded somewhere without a jump start. That's why you'll want Ryobi's 18V Jump Starter. Ryobi's jump starter runs on any 18V ONE+ battery you already own and delivers 1,600 amps of peak power to jump-start a dead battery. That's enough for cars, trucks, SUVs, and even select diesel engines. It features anti-spark technology, a built-in LED, alligator clamps, and a protective battery cover to keep things dry in rain, sleet, or snow. I found one on sale earlier this year, and it's great. I appreciate the built-in handle, LED light, and the peace of mind that it provides. I threw an old 2Ah battery in my truck with this jump starter, and that'll be enough for 20 jumps. Perfect! I'm a huge fan of ice fishing, and I've been lugging a loud, stinky, gas-powered Auger out on the ice since I was a teenager. I've done it by hand, too, which is something no one wants to do. If you live somewhere that requires drilling holes in the ice, whether that's for ice fishing or something else, consider the Ryobi 40V Ice Auger. This thing has a quiet yet powerful brushless motor, and Ryobi says it offers 30% more torque than most gas-powered models. It has an 8-inch blade, which should be more than enough for all your winter adventures. Ryobi says you can drill about 25 holes on a single charge, which is pretty decent. Grab one, enjoy your peaceful cold morning without a loud auger, and catch a big one! For those curious, Ryobi also offers earth augers. Make drilling holes in the ice quick, quiet, and easy with the Ryobi 40V HP brushless 8-inch auger. And that's not all, either. Ryobi makes all sorts of products that are great to have around the house, in your vehicle, or charged up and ready to go for winter. I'd highly recommend that everyone buy Ryobi's 18V High-Pressure Tire Inflator, which goes on sale all the time, because we all know cold weather can drain tire pressure. The company has a pretty great portable power cleaner for spraying salt, mud, and road grime off your vehicle, and don't forget about Ryobi's new Storm Preparation Combo Kit. Stock up before the cold weather rolls in. You'll be glad you did.
